articles.title: Six arrested after anti-migrant protest at marina in Hampshire
articles.summary:
Hundreds of protesters turned out at Gosport thinking that asylum seekers were arriving there

Six people have been arrested after anti-migrant protesters gathered at a marina in Hampshire in…

blocks.text: Six people have been arrested after anti-migrant protesters gathered at a marina in Hampshire in the mistaken belief that a small boat was due to arrive.

Heeding calls from the far-right campaigner Daniel Thomas, hundreds of protesters gathered early on Tuesday evening at Gosport in Hampshire, aiming to disrupt any disembarkation of asylum seekers. The Border Force vessels carrying them landed instead in Dover early on Wednesday.
Thomas, who styles himself as Danny Tommo, spent Tuesday afternoon in a speedboat in the Channel broadcasting his pursuit of the asylum seekers to more than 100,000 people.
He is facing a police inquiry after using a blade to slash an inflatable dinghy in the Channel while a rescue worker was onboard.

Hampshire police said two men from Salisbury, aged 19 and 36, had been arrested on suspicion of aggravated trespass; and four people from Gosport – two men aged 33 and 67, and two women aged 31 and 32 – were held on suspicion of assaulting an emergency worker.
The 67-year-old was also held on suspicion of careless driving.
Police are “conducting inquiries” into footage of Thomas slashing the side of an inflatable boat while a member of a rescue team was still on it, then sailing away shouting “traitors”.
The arrests were made after unions representing Border Force staff discussed security concerns with the Home Office following increasingly aggressive tactics by anti-migrant activists.
The discussions followed attacks on Border Force vehicles and attempts to record and identify staff members by some anti-migrant activists.
The Home Office plans to use public order powers to stop the harassment and possible doxxing of government staff who pick up small-boat arrivals at sea.

Lucy Moreton, of the Immigration Services Union, said: “Following several conversations with the ISU regarding staff safety, the Home Office is working with local police and MoD [Ministry of Defence] to ensure that staff, and migrants, are properly protected using existing police powers and civil service support networks.”

Fran Heathcote, the general secretary of the PCS union which represents border force guards, said: “PCS unreservedly condemns this life-threatening and criminal behaviour. Our members do an important and dangerous job and this inference is reckless in the extreme.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “We have been clear that groups creating fear and intimidating communities cannot be allowed to operate with impunity.
“Police should make full use of the powers available to them to deal robustly with criminality and ensure communities, staff and those in their care are protected.
“Recent events demonstrate the need to learn lessons and adapt our response to new tactics, ensuring police have the tools, intelligence and operational plans needed to act quickly and effectively.”
Some of the protesters in Gosport wore black clothing and face coverings, and chanted “send them back”, wrongly assuming the boat would be guided to the Hampshire coast.
It in fact docked in Dover, Kent, at around 12.30am on Wednesday after 51 people on board reportedly refused help from a French ship and spent 33 hours at sea.
It emerged on Tuesday that a second small boat had arrived on UK shores within the last 24 hours without being detected and intercepted.
The boat reached Samphire Hoe, near Dover, on Tuesday afternoon. Border Security Command has detained 21 migrants so far.
On Monday, five people were detained and passed to Border Security Command after a dinghy made it to shore at Folkestone, also in Kent.
The defence minister Luke Pollard dismissed suggestions the government had lost control of the border.
“Our borders are secure, but we want to make them stronger,” he told LBC Radio, adding that a Home Office investigation was under way into what had happened.
A man was found dead on a beach in northern France on Wednesday, French authorities have said.

In a translated statement, a spokesperson for the Pas-de-Calais prefecture said: “The lifeless body of a man, who appeared to be of African origin, was discovered this morning on the Neufchatel-Hardelot beach.
“An investigation has been launched.”
Some 17,480 migrants have arrived in the UK after crossing the Channel by boat so far this year, including 5,011 since Andy Burnham became prime minister.
The total so far for 2026 is down 46% on the same point last year.

Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, has ordered a review after the Border Force failed to intercept a second dinghy in two days. A government spokesperson said on Wednesday: “Border Security Command officers alongside Kent police have been responding to an incident in Dover.
“Twenty-one individuals have already been detained under a swift enforcement response.
“There is a thorough investigation and it would be inappropriate to comment further.”

articles.title: Could a Left Party government in Berlin expropriate large real estate companies?
articles.summary: The socialist Left Party won the Berlin election partly on the promise to implement the city's 2021 expropriation referendum as a way to solve the city's rent crisis. But can it really happen?

image.caption: The Left Party has always supported the grassroots campaign that led to the 2021 referendum to expropriate property giant Deutsche WohnenImage: Paul Zinken/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The socialist Left Party, which won the Berlin election on September 20, was the only major party on the ballot that said it would implement the results of Berlin's 2021 referendum, when 57.6% of Berliners voted to expropriate the apartments owned by real estate companies that own more than 3,000 units.
But the federal government has said they won't let it happen. So is it even possible? And how did we get here? DW explains:

items: What did the Left Party say about expropriation?

blocks.text: The Left Party was one of the main supporters of a successful, years-long grassroots campaign called "Deutsche Wohnen & Co. enteignen," ("Expropriate Deutsche Wohnen").
Deutsche Wohnen is a major property developer that owns over 140,000 units across Germany, and 100,000 in Berlin alone.

The campaign and the Left Party argued that by expropriating this and a handful of other major companies like it, the Berlin government could put some 270,000 apartments in Berlin into public ownership, and make them available at affordable rent prices. Other estimates put the number at around 240,000.
The argument struck a chord, as surveys showed that housing and rent prices were the biggest concerns for Berlin voters in the recent election.
Some 25% of rented property in Berlin is already in public ownership, through state-owned companies like Berlinovo. The expropriation measure would likely push that up to over 30%.
Berlin has space, so why is housing so expensive?

items: The 2021 referendum — what was the question and what came out of it?

blocks.text: The original referendum, held in September 2021, asked Berliners to vote yes or no on a five-point plan:
- Socializing the apartments owned by the major property companies
- Administration of the properties by a public-law entity
- Administration of the properties with participation from both city officials, renters, and local communities
- Ban on any re-privatization
- Compensation for the property companies "significantly below" the market value of the property
The referendum did not oblige the state government — at the time a coalition of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), the Greens, and the Left Party — to immediately implement the plan.

Instead, the then-SPD Mayor Franziska Giffey put together a 13-person expert commission, including former justice ministers and constitutional law experts. This was given the task of establishing whether the plan conformed with the German constitution, or Basic Law, and how the compensation could be organized.
In 2023, the commission concluded that expropriation was legal and possible, though budget questions still needed to be clarified.

By then, a new conservative-led government, headed by the Christian Democratic Union's (CDU) Kai Wegner, had been voted into office, and announced that it would not expropriate any real estate companies, regardless of what the commission said. At the same time, it emerged that the Berlin CDU was receiving hundreds of thousands of euros in donations from property companies.

Instead, the government said it would draw up a socialization law that would define the conditions for the socialization of property, while ruling out expropriation. A draft law was completed in December 2025.

The Deutsche Wohnen Enteignen campaign rejected this idea as pointless, and had in the meantime gathered legal experts to draw up its own expropriation and socialization law, and promised to start another campaign to force a referendum to implement that.

items: The legal basis for expropriation: Articles 14 and 15 of the German constitution

blocks.text: The original campaign founded its plan on articles 14 and 15 of the German Basic Law.
Article 14 says that, while the right to property is guaranteed, "expropriation shall only be permissible for the public good."

Article 15 states: "Land, natural resources and means of production may, for the purpose of nationalization, be transferred to public ownership or other forms of public enterprise by a law that determines the nature and extent of compensation."
As far as the campaigners are concerned, the law they have drawn up covers those two bases.

But, while Article 14 is implemented often enough (for example, when the state wants to build a new highway), Article 15 has never been implemented at all. It is new legal territory, and no one is quite sure what would happen if it were tried.

Some legal experts say the plan would contravene European law. Housing companies would almost certainly fight the measure in court and demand more compensation than the government is willing to offer.
Business Beyond: The global housing crisis

items: 'Not happening' — Chancellor Merz vows to prevent expropriation

blocks.text: Chancellor Friedrich Merz responded to the Left Party's election victory immediately by promising to draw up a federal law banning state governments from expropriating property.

"It's not just about banning something here in Berlin," Merz said at a press conference in the aftermath of the Berlin election. "It's about sending a clear message to international investors, which is: There is no expropriation of private property in Germany."

However, it's unclear whether the federal government has the power to impose such a law. Germany's Constitutional Court once ruled that the federal government cannot pass a law simply to prevent a state from governing in the issues it wants.

items: What now?

blocks.text: The Left Party still has to enter into coalition negotiations to form a government in Berlin. Its most likely coalition partners are the SPD and the Greens, and given the opposition from the federal government and the massive controversy over the issue, the expropriation plan could become a major sticking point.

Whatever happens, the Left Party itself acknowledges that expropriation and socialization would take a while to put into practice, and it would be even longer before it had a measurable effect on Berlin's overall rents.
In the meantime, it has drawn up a number of laws that it hopes will tackle the problem more quickly, such as a rent cap.

In any case, Berliners themselves appear to have gone a little cold on the idea. Despite the Left's electoral success, a recent poll by infratest-dimap found that only 37% of Berliners are still in favor of expropriating real estate companies.
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

articles.title: Nike cofounder gives $1bn to University of Oregon in historic donation
articles.summary:
Phil Knight and wife, Penny, make largest known donation to a flagship university to fund a new engineering school

Nike cofounder Phil Knight, and his wife, Penny, have donated $1bn to the…

blocks.text: Nike cofounder Phil Knight, and his wife, Penny, have donated $1bn to the University of Oregon in what is believed to be the largest known donation to a flagship university.
The donation, which was first reported by local Oregon media and the New York Times, will go toward the creation of a new engineering school in Eugene.

The University of Oregon’s president, Karl Scholz, said in a statement to local Oregon outlet LookOut Eugene-Springfield on Wednesday morning that the Knights have “a long history of believing in things before they exist” and that “they did it in 2016, and they are doing it again now, at a scale that is genuinely hard to take in. I am grateful to them, and I am grateful to be here for it.”
In the announcement, Knight also shared a statement noting that “to make an audacious dream a reality requires more than a vivid imagination”.
“It also requires the sort of opportunity that our great American universities, both public and private, have historically provided,” he said. “This is no time to abandon them.”
He added: “Penny and I are grateful for the chance to invest in our most promising young people’s future in this important way.”
Knight, 88, is a graduate of the university. The latest donation brings the Knight family’s known total giving to the University of Oregon to more than $2bn, according to the New York Times.

Scholz said in an interview with the New York Times about the donation that “one of the most successful businesspeople in the history of humanity, and one of the most generous philanthropists in the history of humanity, has said higher education is worth an investment of this magnitude.
“At a time when we’re all feeling a little bit under siege, this is tremendous news,” he said, adding that the gift amounted to “a screaming endorsement of the importance of what we’re doing”.
The University of Oregon did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian about the donation.

Bob Guldberg, a vice-president at the university who is also a professor of bioengineering, also told the New York Times that the $1bn donation will allow the university to establish a full undergraduate program that could help address a shortage of engineers in the state.

The news on Wednesday comes as earlier this month it was announced that the Knights were committing $1.1bn to Providence St Vincent Medical Center and to Providence Heart Institute to create Oregon’s first hospital dedicated exclusively to women’s health.

“Penny and I have always believed that real breakthroughs come from people willing to take on the toughest challenges,” Knight said in a statement earlier this month. “Providence has shown that kind of ambition in cardiovascular care, and we see the same opportunity to do something truly distinctive for women’s health. We’re proud to invest in teams that will change what’s possible for communities across Oregon and beyond.”

Last year, Oregon Health & Science University announced that it had received a $2bn commitment from the Knights to its cancer institute, which the university said would “transform the future of cancer care and set a new standard globally”.

articles.title: Ottawa city council votes to dump Trump Avenue
articles.summary: Ottawa city council voted Wednesday to rename a street that was named after U.S. President Donald Trump more than 20 years ago.

image.caption: Trump Avenue is in Ottawa's Central Park neighbourhood where several streets are named after New York City landmarks. (Francis Ferland/CBC)

blocks.text: Ottawa·New
Ottawa city council voted Wednesday to rename a street that was named after U.S. President Donald Trump more than 20 years ago.
City councillor objected to honouring U.S. president in light of Trump's threats to Canada
River ward Coun. Riley Brockington moved to change the name of Trump Avenue at the Sept. 9 city council meeting, saying Trump does not deserve the honour in light of his repeated threats to Canada.
His motion was approved without comment from anyone but Brockington, who said it was time for a new beginning for the street's residents.

Brockington said he will now lead a public consultation process to select a new name for the street in the Central Park neighbourhood off Merivale Road, which includes other New York City-themed names such as Bloomingdale Street and Staten Way.
Brockington said Trump Avenue's new name could stick to that theme.
A working group will be formed to go over options, Brockington said. The goal is to have a new name for the next city council to vote on by April, May or June of next year.

His motion came after Trump imposed tariffs on many billions of dollars worth of Canadian goods and signed an order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America. Canada has retaliated with tariffs on an equivalent value of U.S. imports.

A previous effort to rename Trump Avenue in 2021 fell through after a consultation found residents split on the idea, with many who opposed the change expressing concerns about the inconvenience of changing their home address.
With files from Arthur White-Crummey

articles.title: Azerbaijan pardons Frenchman after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire
articles.summary: Martin Ryan is pardoned months after he was jailed on charges of spying, but a second Frenchman remains in prison.

blocks.text: French national Martin Ryan has been pardoned and his release from prison ordered by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev after he was jailed on charges of spying.

His release came hours after the EU agreed to lift sanctions on two Russian billionaires, prompting anger from Ukraine. Diplomats had indicated that France had pushed for an end to restrictions on one of the businessmen, Alisher Usmanov.
Ryan, who denied espionage, is one of 20 people pardoned by Aliyev.
However, a second Frenchman, Anass Derraz, remains in jail in Azerbaijan accused of accepting a Russian bribe.
It was not clear what had led to pressure for sanctions on Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov to be lifted - the EU also agreed to take Russian-Israeli oligarch Mikhail Fridman off its sanctions list.
Slovakia is understood to have pressed for Usmanov's name to removed initially, and France then backed the move, highlighting national security concerns.

Both men have been under EU embargo since the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and until now EU sanctions on more than 3,000 "individuals and entities" have had to be renewed every six months. The latest agreement extends the sanctions on the others for three years.

Usmanov was cited by the EU in its 2022 listing, external as having "particularly close ties" to Russia's President Vladimir Putin, and of having "supported materially or financially and benefited from Russian decision-makers responsible for the annexation of Crimea and the destabilisation of Ukraine".
The metals and mining billionaire denied this characterisation of him. He has also been sanctioned by the UK and US governments.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha bitterly criticised the EU decision to lift sanctions on the two men, complaining that Moscow was "celebrating, because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans".
Latvia had initially opposed the move, but decided to abstain, announcing instead that it would impose its own measures on the two men.

Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said it was "dangerous and sends completely the wrong signal at a time when Russia's behaviour is becoming more aggressive". Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said later that France's President Emmanuel Macron had agreed to start talks on Latvia's "accession to the French nuclear deterrence initiative".

French relations with Azerbaijan have been poor in recent years, largely because of France's close relations with neighbouring Armenia. However, in May, Macron discussed developing ties with Aliyev, who later spoke of a "new era" in their relations.
Under Aliyev's decree on Wednesday, Ryan is one of 20 people including Azerbaijanis and Turks given a pardon.
Detained in December 2023, he was handed a 10-year jail term last March for espionage, charges denied by the French government.

Prosecutors alleged he had co-operated with employees of France's security services in Baku and gathered information about Azerbaijan's relations with Turkey, Iran and Pakistan, as well as companies linked to Russia and China.
"I did not spy. I am not a spy, and during the court case I tried to prove this," Ryan had told the court.
Another man he went on trial with, Azad Mamedli, was given 12 years in jail. Mamedli was not among the 20 prisoners pardoned by Aliyev.

articles.title: The EU’s Canada offer is more mood than reality but it could hint at a future geometry for the bloc
articles.summary: While Brussels and Ottawa desire a deeper partnership born of Trump-era volatility, ​the EU has no legal framework to accommodate it

blocks.text: The EU and Canada, Ursula von der Leyen said last week, “see the world with the same eyes”, with shared stances on everything from AI to the climate crisis, the Ukraine war and the unholy chaos unleashed by the current occupant of the White House (OK, she didn’t actually say that last bit. But I like to think she almost certainly thought it.)

So, the European Commission president went on, Canada should become “the first associate member of the EU”. In the audience, Mark Carney beamed with delight. The next day, Canada’s prime minister enthusiastically embraced the idea of an “alliance for the future”, to build “collective resilience” through “deep cooperation”.

Cue standing ovations, warm handshakes – and a great deal of head-scratching in Brussels and assorted EU capitals. Because “associate membership” of the EU is not, in fact, a thing. Nor, as a Guardian editorial pointed out, is there “any blueprint for what such a thing might involve”.

The term was, the editorial argued, “a political hypothesis”, describing “a relationship of intimate strategic alignment with the EU, stopping short of actual membership, in ways that are significant but undefined”. So what exactly are the commission and Canada playing at here, and where might it lead?

You can see where they’re coming from. On paper, in a world of unpredictable and increasingly aggressive great powers, it makes perfect sense. For Canada – which already has the Ceta free trade agreement with the EU – the catalyst for even closer cooperation is clearly Donald Trump: incessant tariff threats, an escalating trade war, bullying talk of Canada as the “51st state”, the renaming of Lake Ontario – all have left Ottawa eager to diversify its relations.

Aligning with European industrial strategy, working together on defence and AI, and joining EU scientific research and student exchange programmes would offer Canada a reliable counterweight to its all-too-unreliable southern neighbour. (Unsurprisingly, Trump called the tie-up “laughable”, and threatened more tariffs.)

For the EU, meanwhile, Canada is a dream partner: a stable, like-minded “middle power” rich in critical minerals, rare earths and – as Carney couldn’t resist noting – good manners. Plus, Canada’s unbridled EU-enthusiasm is a pleasing boost to the bloc’s bruised ego after Iceland’s recent rejection of more EU accession negotiations.

There’s only one problem: “associate membership” is not a status in the EU treaties, and creating such a status would mean treaty reform, which member states won’t contemplate. There are things called “association agreements”, such as with Ukraine, Moldova or Georgia, but those are essentially stepping stones to full membership – which Canada can’t aspire to, for the very good reason that it isn’t in Europe.

But if “associate member” sounds vaguely familiar, that’s because the EU has been talking about a “second circle” since the days of Jacques Delors: an outer ring of countries bound by shared values, free trade and security cooperation to an inner core of members, but without full voting rights or complete regulatory integration.

Emmanuel Macron’s European Political Community is a variation on this theme, and Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, recently floated “associate member” status for Ukraine. Indeed, non-EU nations in the European Economic Area (EEA) and European Free Trade Association, such as Norway, Iceland or Switzerland, already function as quasi-associate members, enjoying single-market access while being largely “rule-takers”: adopting EU rules without having a vote in Brussels.

Writing in the Guardian, Fabian Zuleeg suggested that Canada and Europe actually need more of an “integrated partnership” – a model that leaves single market access to one side, focusing instead on concrete collaboration in areas such as defence, supply chains and EU programmes like Horizon and Erasmus+.

Alberto Alemanno, a professor of EU law, noted that a realistic EU-Canada landing zone would have to go further than Ceta and might more resemble the kind of tailored framework of the EU-Swiss relationship. But the real significance of any formal new status, he said, was that it could make the EU “an institutional hub around which other democracies organise strategic autonomy – but without joining the union”.

What that might actually look like is anyone’s guess: visa-free work access, shared military procurement, Canadian seats on EU regulatory committees? For the moment, Canada’s hypothetical “associate membership” is more of a mood than a reality: the expressed intent of a democratic bloc and a middle power to deepen ties in the face of mounting global uncertainty.

Does it, all the same, hold any hope for Brexit-regretting Britain? As Jill Rutter of the Institute for Government highlighted, the EU’s sudden willingness to display “institutional imagination” at least shows that the bloc is willing to think about adapting when geopolitical pressures demand.

But a new deal for Canada won’t automatically fix the UK’s issues. As Joël Reland of UK in a Changing Europe pointed out, the vagueness of the EU offer to Canada might look promising for the UK. But Canada wants “deep cooperation” without touching single-market rules, and the UK’s main problem is that it is now shut out of that same market. Whatever Canada eventually gets, it’s unlikely to work for the UK.
after newsletter promotion
A miserable time for Merz

blocks.caption: Friedrich Merz needs to rethink policy in order to stay on top. Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters

blocks.text: Friedrich Merz is in trouble. A fortnight after the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) swept to a crushing victory in one state election in Saxony-Anhalt, the German chancellor’s centre-right CDU failed to clear the 5% threshold needed to enter the state parliament in another, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

It fared a little better in Berlin, where it was the incumbent, but was still beaten – by a clear five-point margin – by the far-left Die Linke. And the AfD made headway in the capital, too, surging to a double-digit result. The embattled chancellor has vowed to fight on, but faces an uncomfortable choice: revise the unpopular economic reforms he insists are essential, or risk oblivion defending them.

Meanwhile, as long as he refuses to step aside and no one is actively seeking to replace him, a volatile and damaging deadlock will reign in Europe’s biggest economy. After 16 months in office, it is becoming increasingly clear – as a Guardian editorial noted – that Merz is “ill-suited for the job” of defending Germany’s democratic future against the far right.

articles.title: Britain to join the EU’s new global ocean monitoring system
articles.summary:
Cooperation on OceanEye, which will help to predict extreme weather and climate events, comes amid government attempts to move closer to Brussels

Britain is to join a major new ocean science…

blocks.text: Britain is to join a major new ocean science programme, led by the EU, to better forecast extreme weather and climate events, it will announce today in New York.

The announcement comes as Andy Burnham’s government aims to rebuild the UK’s relationship with Europe, and follows warnings that this year’s “supersized” El Niño, tracked in the Pacific Ocean, will fuel more extreme weather globally.

Scientists have warned that the global marine monitoring system, which is vital to predict extreme weather events and ultimately to save lives, is under strain after threats by the US administration this year to dismantle its substantial share of global ocean observations.

In June, the EU launched a €92m (£78m) initiative called OceanEye, to boost its role in ocean observation and to provide data-backed marine intelligence to deepen understanding and management of the ocean. It plans to create a digital “real time” replica model of the ocean, collected by satellites, sensors and other models by 2030, to help decisions on ocean protection and security. The EU introduced an international alliance with Canada as part of OceanEye, to address critical gaps in under-monitored regions and strengthen cooperation between nations.
In addition to weather and climate predictions, ocean observations also underpin national security, global trade and marine protections.

The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, will announce the UK is to join the scheme at the headquarters of the United Nations in New York at a meeting attended by the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, and Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister.
Britain will share more data from the Met Office and other agencies with the EU and Canada than before.

Eagle will tell the event: “As an island nation and a global leader in climate science, we know that data from ocean monitoring is essential to our ability to protect and restore our oceans, and anticipate and respond to the huge threats they face, because we cannot save our oceans if we do not understand them.”

“Changing weather patterns and currents are fuelling the extreme weather which is already impacting all of our nations – through floods, droughts, storms and extreme heat. That’s why the UK is so committed to maintaining our vital global network of observation systems, which span coastal waters, shelf seas and the open ocean, including some of the longest-running observations in the world.”

Joining the alliance to support and provide data to the Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) would help better protect Britain from the impacts of climate change, said the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. Currently, the global ocean observing capacity has significant gaps, at the poles, the deep ocean and of biological measurements.

The US, which provides over half the ocean observing platforms and much of the technology, has reversed a proposal to scrap its $368m (£275m) funding for its Ocean Observatories Initiative after a backlash from scientists. However, moves to cut funding for US ocean agencies have left GOOS vulnerable to changing priorities of the US administration.

articles.title: Burnham stands by claim that UK is ‘in hock’ to bond markets
articles.summary: PM says his comments last year were deliberately misinterpreted by Keir Starmer and his advisers

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has said he still believes the UK is far too exposed to global shocks, defending comments last year when he said the UK should be less “in hock” to the bond markets.

He said the comments had been deliberately misinterpreted by the former prime minister Keir Starmer and his advisers and said his aim was not more borrowing and spending but a far more resilient economy.

Burnham’s comments in an interview with the New Statesmen last year made waves before the Labour conference because of the then Greater Manchester’s clear ambitions to replace Starmer as prime minister.

In a fresh interview with the magazine on Wednesday, he said he had intended to highlight how vulnerable the UK was to global price fluctuations. Government borrowing has climbed again over the past months as energy prices have risen in response to continued deadlock on the Iran war.

blocks.caption: This week’s New Statesman cover. Photograph: New Statesman

blocks.text: The UK government borrowed a higher than expected £18.3bn last month, putting further pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, as he prepares for next month’s budget.

Burnham said he wanted to build an economy that was far less vulnerable. “I mean, the point about the bond markets, it holds – in that what I was saying was the country has left itself over-exposed,” he said, telling the magazine he was arguing for a “much more streamlined, productive state”.

He said criticism from Starmer and the then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, was unjustified. “They couldn’t understand why I was saying some of the things that I was saying … [They] didn’t know what to do with it, but they did what they always do, which is they pulled one line out of it and then framed that one line within their world, rather than the one that I was talking about.”

Burnham also addressed criticism from the Conservatives after he said during an exchange at prime minister’s questions that national security “should not come at the expense of social security” – which opponents said showed he was not willing to cut the welfare budget to fund increased defence spending.
“It oversimplifies the political discourse that we need to have, doesn’t it?” he said.

Burnham, who will address his first Labour conference as prime minister in Liverpool next Tuesday, said he would set out his political vision, which would be a break from the economic and political mainstream of the past 40 years.
“It’s about control,” he said. “If you strip it back, and all the fluff and, you know, the verbiage, you can actually strip it back to one word, which is control.”

He said that would be a business-friendly approach, rather than purely statist. “People aren’t going to come in and invest in a significant way where the place isn’t functional and it’s in major decline,” he said, saying it was the state’s job to “create the optimum conditions for private-sector investment”.
“We’ve just got to get that belief back into Britain that, yeah, we know what we’re about, we know what we stand for, that is what we’ve always been, so we can do it again.”

In attempts to calm jittery bond markets, Burnham has previously said his budget would “stick to the fiscal rules” on debt and borrowing set out under Reeves, “but at the same time we will help reduce cost of living pressure on our constituents”.

articles.title: China's 13-year-old swimming star raises questions on child athletes
articles.summary: Three gold medals and three Asian Games records have catapulted China's Yu Zidi, 13, into the sporting spotlight. She is far from the first teen prodigy, but should teens be competing at elite level?

image.caption: Yu Zidi has won three golds and set three Games records at the Asian GamesImage: Wu Zhizun/Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: The third Asian Games gold medal looked as convincing as the first two, even if Yu Zidi insisted that: "It didn't feel easy at all. It was quite challenging."

On Wednesday, the 13-year-old Chinese swimmer broke the Games record for the third time to add the women's 400 meter individual medley title to her golds in the 200 meter medley and 200 meter butterfly. The three medals add to a bronze she won last year at the World Championships.

Even two years out from the Los Angeles Olympics, talk is turning to a potential rivalry with Canada's Summer McIntosh, 20, who herself finished fourth in the 2020 Olympics at 14 and won a world title at 15. As well as their remarkable talent, the pair's youth has raised some questions.
"The first reaction you have when you see something like this is you think, wow, there's a big career ahead," three-time open water swimming world champion Leonie Beck, of Germany, told DW.

blocks.caption: Summer McIntosh is the only person to have swum faster than Yu Zidi in the 400 meters individual medleyImage: Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press/picture alliance

blocks.text: "But I think maybe this is the problem. People around [the athlete], or maybe the media can create this pressure on a young talent. But just because you're really good and fast at this age, doesn't mean that your whole career will continue like this."
Early success is not always sustained

Beck has already retired from elite competition at 29 and swimming is a sport where athletes often peak early. Katie Ledecky, of the US, and Japan's Kyoko Iwasaki both won Olympic gold at 15 and Japan's Yumeki Kojima, 17, has been a home favorite at the Asian Games, winning a gold and silver in the pool.
While the temptation is to think of Yu as a prodigy, Beck said that to reach the level she has also requires extraordinary dedication and sacrifice.

"My first international competition was in 2011 [at age 14]. At that stage already, I was training eight times a week. You wake up at 5 a.m., by 6 you're in the pool, out at 7:30 so you're in school at 8:00, school until 1, going home, eating, maybe doing some homework, going back in the water training at 3. Then one hour of dry land [training], then in the water again and coming back home at 7 (p.m.). I had this when I was young too."

blocks.caption: Leonie Beck won three world and three European titlesImage: Oliver Weiken/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Yu, who was discovered by chance by a swimming coach at a water park aged 6, admitted in an interview with state media Xinhua at an event in China in January that the workload takes its toll.
"Being in class all day and still having to train was really tiring," she said. "Sometimes I was so tired I could fall asleep even while eating."

While, for Beck, the sporting success made such struggles worthwhile, not all athletes who dedicate their childhoods to their sport reach the pinnacle. The German swimmer added that putting educational, physical and mental support structures in place is critical for sports that allow under-18s to compete.
"Sport psychology should start at a really young age because it should be normal, the same as physiotherapists," she said. "Especially at a young age, where sport should be also fun."

World Aquatics rules state that the minimum age for international championships is 14 but exceptions can be made for those fast enough, like Yu. While swimmers peak earlier than athletes in other sports, teenagers at the top level are not so unusual.

In football, Lamine Yamal won the Euros with Spain at 16, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, of India, made his debut in cricket's Indian Premier League at 13 and Nadia Comaneci, of Romania, became the first gymnast to be awarded a perfect 10 in the 1976 Olympics in Montreal aged 14.
Neither are young athletes a modern phenomenon. Dimitrios Loundras remains the youngest ever Olympic medallist, winning a bronze with the Greek gymnastics team in 1896.

While support structures in sport are improving, challenges remain, according to Rosemary Purcell, who played a part in the International Olympic Committee's (IOC) review into youth development ahead of the Paris Olympics in 2024.
"There are pretty stark differences between what we see in the community and in these elite youth athletes," Purcell told DW during those Games.

"Some sports do have a higher rate of eating disorders and body image disturbance in young athletes, but conversely, they may have lower rates of depression and anxiety than we would see in the community."
If you're good enough, you're old enough?
In general, sporting bodies tend to take the approach that if an athlete is good enough, they are old enough. Beck said, allied with the right support, this approach is correct.

"Every athlete has completely different development. Why should you take away the success of a young athlete just because she's young and successful in that age? In my opinion, you should give her the possibility to be successful at that age because maybe, who knows, in a later stage of her career, she will be not that successful. It's not just a solution to say: 'look, you're that age, you're not able to compete.'"

But she also cautioned that because success won't always last, young elite sportspeople should be helped to find a plan away from the pitch, pool or mat, something she struggled somewhat with post Paris 2024.

"You have this idea that, ok, I want to reach the Olympic Games, win this medal. So you have a structure of where to go, what to do. And at one point it's gone and you're like, ‘ok, but now what am I doing with my life? What do I want to reach? What are my goals?'
"It's really, really important that people are starting to think that, 'hey, we are also human beings and you should do something to have a life after the sport because the sport is not endless.'"

articles.title: New York and Boston face weekend nor’easter with high winds
articles.summary:
First such storm of fall could have wind gusts of 70mph in places, flooding and power outages, forecasters warn

New York, Boston, and much of New England could face a weekend nor’easter…

blocks.text: New York, Boston, and much of New England could face a weekend nor’easter storm with wind gusts of 70mph in places, and “significant” impacts including beach erosion, flooding, and power outages, forecasters warn.

Effects from the season’s first such storm since Tuesday’s official start of fall could last through the weekend, especially if the system sits swirling off the coast, a scenario experts say is looking increasingly likely.

“If the storm nearly stalls, several days of persistent onshore winds and pounding surf could take a significant toll on beaches and vulnerable coastal communities, especially with astronomical high tides coinciding,” said Alyssa Glenney, an AccuWeather meteorologist.

The online weather service predicted “a long-duration storm for many areas along the mid-Atlantic and New England coasts”, with impacts beginning late Wednesday, spreading to New England late Friday or Saturday, and lasting through Sunday in some places.

The Weather Channel said coastal flood alerts were in place across the mid-Atlantic, and winds were likely to bring sea rise up to 3ft above normal levels. But it said uncertainty remained about exactly where the system would be at the end of the week.
“Forecast models are picking up on the low, but two models show that the timing and duration of the storm could differ,” the Weather Channel said on its website, weather.com.

“The European model brings the low close to the coast as a strong storm, but it moves slower. It could even meander around the east coast until it fizzles. Under this scenario, there would be more time for strong winds to cause significant power outages, heavy rain-induced flooding, and coastal erosion.”
The GFS model, meanwhile, brings the storm in faster, and approaching New England by Saturday afternoon.

“A faster storm could mean winds, rain and coastal erosion would be less severe and lessen disruptions to travel and weekend plans,” the Weather Channel said. “However, this model calls for a stronger storm by the end of the weekend as it moves away from the north east, meaning some coastal areas could experience longer-lasting impacts.”

Nor’easters are more prevalent from September to April, the National Weather Service said. They usually develop within about 100 miles of the cost between Georgia and New Jersey, and progress steadily north eastward, typically attaining maximum intensity near New England and the maritime provinces of Canada.
AccuWeather’s forecasters agreed with the Weather Channel that the exact track of this weekend’s storm remained important for communities farther inland.

“A track closer to the coast could bring heavier rain, stronger wind gusts and travel disruptions from Washington DC and Philadelphia, to New York City and Boston, while a track farther offshore would limit inland rain and wind impacts,” the service said.

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 29: Court overturns initial 16-conviction threshold in VP trial
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court on Wednesday voted to base the two-thirds vote to convict the impeached Vice President Sara Duterte on the number of senators who are capable of "legally and factually…

blocks.text: The Senate impeachment court on Wednesday voted to base the two-thirds vote to convict the impeached Vice President Sara Duterte on the number of senators who are capable of "legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings."

Thirteen senator-judges voted in favor of the motion put forward by Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo, who sought reconsideration of the July 6 ruling after some senators became unavailable to participate in the impeachment trial.
On July 6, presiding officer Senator-judge Francis "Chiz" Escudero set the number of votes needed to convict at 16, or two-thirds of all the 24 senators.
Article 11, Section 6 of the Constitution does not state a number and instead reads, "No person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate.”
The same constitutional provision also states that "The Senate shall have the sole power to try and decide all cases of impeachment."
Those who voted in favor of Tulfo’s motion are:

items: Paolo Benigno "Bam" Aquino IV
JV Ejercito
Sherwin Gatchalian
Risa Hontiveros
Panfilo Lacson
Lito Lapid
Francis Pangilinan
Vicente "Tito" Sotto III
Erwin Tulfo
Raffy Tulfo
Joel Villanueva
Mark Villar
Juan Miguel Zubiri

blocks.text: Of the 13, only Senator Villar is from the Minority bloc.
The lone no vote came from Escudero.
The six minority bloc senators who did not participate in the vote are:

items: Alan Peter Cayetano
Pia Cayetano
Christopher Go
Imee Marcos
Robin Padilla
Camille Villar

blocks.text: Defense team lead counsel Sheila Sison said the Vice President’s camp will exhaust all legal remedies to address the new threshold for conviction, among other things.

"She reserves every right to exhaust all legal remedies available sa ilalim ng ating batas at Konstitusyon na may pagtatangi sa esensya ng isang tunay na malayang, demokratikong institusyon. At karapatan ng bawat mamamayan na madinig sa isang hukuman na walang kinikilingan o kinakatakutan," she added.

(She reserves every right to exhaust all legal remedies available under our law and Constitution, with due regard for the essence of a truly free, democratic institution. And it is the right of every citizen to be heard in an impartial court that fears no one.)
Alan Cayetano attempted to defer the voting, to no avail.
No acquittal by default

Ahead of the vote, House prosecutor Chel Diokno of Akbayan party-list said the threshold must be changed since the Vice President’s case should be decided on merits, not by default or absence of senator-judges.

“Yes, the Constitution deliberately makes conviction harder by imposing the two-thirds requirement. But making it harder is not the same as making it depend on senators who are not judges or who are incapable of acting as judges. That would be tantamount to an acquittal by default, a failure to arrive at the threshold number caused not by the judgment of the incapacitated senators, but by their mere inclusion in the denominator,” Diokno added.
Defense counsel Michael Poa, however, said that the July 6 ruling of Escudero setting 16 votes as the threshold cannot be appealed since it is not provided under Senate impeachment rules.

“Last July 6, 2026, on the very first day of trial, the presiding officer ruled that a voting threshold to convict is 16. At that time, no senator-judge objected. No senator-judge sought reconsideration. No senator-judge appealed. Your Honors, that was over two months ago. There is no supervening event. Our point is, nothing changed between July 6 and today,” Poa said.

Escudero, however, had a rebuttal for Poa by citing the Supreme Court decision in People v. Amigo, GR number 116719, which states that Supreme Court decisions are “not petrified rules grown rigid once pronounced, but may be reconsidered upon further reflection in light of new perspectives.”

“The July ruling issued during an ongoing proceeding is not a final judgment on any Article of Impeachment. It cannot claim greater; therefore, this issue cannot claim greater immutability than the judicial doctrine itself. Where the governing impeachment rules prescribe no period and no final judgment has been rendered, the court remains free to reconsider its interpretation,” Escudero said.

Erwin Tulfo also addressed Poa’s comments that there is no supervening event, citing that their four colleagues being detained due to alleged plunder, being in hiding from authorities and being on leave are something that the court should address as elected representatives of the people.
Camille Villar then appealed to his colleagues not to attack their detained fellow senators, saying that they are not yet convicted of their alleged crimes.
Her take was seconded by his brother, Mark Villar, citing that there should be respect among colleagues.
Erwin Tulfo apologized if his comments offended his colleagues, but he stressed that he never said their colleagues were convicted of crimes.
“What I said was they were charged in court,” Tulfo said.

“Further, the statements were not attacks against our fellow senators but merely confronting the present reality that some senators are physically or legally unable to participate in the impeachment trial. The issue of detained senators is so intertwined in the determination of the denominator,” Tulfo added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Young Australians are staying in the family home for longer – and it’s not hard to see why
articles.summary:
Housing costs are up with renters worst affected and financial stress is also growing, according to the largest survey of its type

  • Get our

blocks.text: Every year, thousands of Australians answer a series of questions as part of the long-running Hilda survey.
This questionnaire – more expansively known as the household, income and labour dynamics in Australia survey – has been tracking the same households since 2001.

As the families have expanded over the past two decades, the survey has grown to include about 17,000 people a year in 9,000 households, offering a unique insight into Australian life in the 21st century – and how it has changed.
This week, the Melbourne Institute of Applied Economic and Social Research, which manages the survey, published its annual snapshot of the social and economic trends shaping Australia.
Here are six things we learned.
Half of young Australians are living with their parents
The trend is clear: leaving the nest has become ever harder.
In 2001, 39% of people aged 18-29 were living at home with their folks. Fast forward to 2024, and that figure is just shy of 50%.
Young men are more likely to live at home than women, but that gap has shrunk a bit over the 23 years. And 36% of 18- to 29-year-olds living at home in 2024 are full-time students.
It’s also notable that the big shift towards staying at home happened through the first decade of the century.
More of us studying for longer is one answer, but so is the mounting cost of moving out, which we’ll turn to a bit further below.
One group is being left behind
Employment rates reached record highs in 2024, with the survey showing 84.4% of working-age men and 76% of working-age women had jobs.
Aussie workers are better educated – more than half of women aged 25-44 now hold a university degree.
Men are better educated now than at the start of the century, too, but in every age group women were found to be “considerably better educated than men,” the report said.
But there is one group where employment outcomes have become much worse.
As Kyle Peyton, a co-author of the report, says: “Men aged 25 to 44 who did not complete year 12 have become less likely to be in full-time work and more likely to be outside the labour force”.
“Their full-time employment rate fell from 70% in 2001 to 63% in 2024, while the share outside the labour force rose from 12% to 22%,” Peyton says.
Women who never finished high school – and did not achieve any other higher education – have also dropped out of the workforce at greater rates: from 40% in 2001, to 48% in 2024.
That’s not as sharp an increase, but still much higher than for men.
Household income has trended higher this decade …
The pandemic, the huge lockdown payments from governments, and the post-Covid inflationary outbreak has made for a bumpy ride.

Median disposable (or after tax) household incomes peaked in 2021, before being pummelled by soaring living costs from 2022. The Hilda survey shows the typical household was earning less in 2024 than the recent peak in 2021, but more than in 2019.
Looking longer term, the survey shows household incomes lifted strongly through the first decade of the century, before plateauing right up to the pandemic.
… but financial wellbeing is down
Australians report lower financial wellbeing on average than they did before Covid-19, despite higher median household incomes.
As Inga Lass, the lead author of the report, says “the post-pandemic shock to cost-of-living is clear”.
There were declines in reported financial wellbeing across age groups between 2020 and 2024 – except for the over-65s.

The survey asked five questions and asked people how well it described them from one (“not at all”) to five (“completely”). The researchers then converted this to a wellbeing score out of 100 (where the higher the number, the higher the wellbeing).

The share of people who could enjoy life “not at all” or “very little” due to their money management lifted from 11.3% in 2020 to 12.7% in 2024. And in 2020, 62.1% agreed or strongly agreed that they felt on top of everyday finances; by 2024 it was 58.5%.
And while 60% of people in 2020 agreed or strongly agreed they were comfortable with their current spending relative to the money coming in, that share had dropped to 53.8% in 2024.

“These results imply that worsening perceptions of meeting shorter-term ‘every day’ financial outcomes explain a sizeable shift in the reported decline in financial wellbeing over the four-year period,” the report said.
Housing costs are higher …
Of course, we all know that the cost of keeping a roof over your head (and your family’s) has been a major factor in the new era of high living costs.
The Hilda survey shows weekly mortgage payments – including principal and interest – jumped between 2021 and 2024 to reach new highs as the Reserve Bank jacked up interest rates.
Fast forward to today, and the RBA has reversed the three rate cuts it made in 2025, which means the burden on mortgage holders is similar to when the last survey took place.
The survey shows weekly private rental costs were pretty steady through the 2010s, but have since climbed higher and higher.
And while overall household incomes are lower than they were in 2021, housing costs are higher – which has heaped pressure on many Australians.
Housing stress is particularly acute for renters in the regions
The Hilda survey uses the “30-40 rule” to measure housing stress.
A household is in housing stress if housing costs are more than 30% of disposable household income, and the household is in the bottom 40% of households by disposable income.
Among the cities, renters in Sydney are the most likely to be experiencing housing stress, with more than 31% meeting the definition in 2024 – that’s about twice the rate in Adelaide.
The next toughest market is in Brisbane, with 26% of renters in housing stress. Across the mainland capital cities, one in four are in housing stress.
As high as those rates are, the share of regional renters in housing stress is substantially higher at 30%, and nearly double what it was before the pandemic.
In contrast, about one in 10 mortgaged owners are in housing stress, and that number has generally held steady over the past 20-plus years.

items: Patrick Commins is Guardian Australia’s economics editor

articles.title: Coogee ranks as Sydney’s worst ocean beach for faecal pollution – again
articles.summary:
Seventy-nine per cent of all NSW swimming sites rated ‘good’ or ‘very good’, as state’s cleanest and most polluted beaches revealed

  • Get our

blocks.text: Coogee has ranked as the Sydney ocean beach most polluted with faecal matter, an annual state survey has found.

Of 245 swimming sites across New South Wales, 43 sites (17.6%) received a rating of “poor” or “very poor” in the 2026 State of the Beaches report, part of an annual survey by the state’s environment department.
Coogee’s grading – unchanged from last year – indicates “microbial water quality is susceptible to faecal pollution, particularly after rainfall and occasionally during dry weather conditions”.
Across NSW, 97% of oceans beaches achieved a “good” or “very good” rating.
Prof Stuart Khan, a water quality expert and head of the School of Civil Engineering at the University of Sydney, said Coogee’s “poor” rating was unsurprising and was largely weather dependent.

Storm water runoff to beaches brings bacterial pollution via several sources, washing dog poo from streets and bird droppings from roofs. Sydney’s sewers were also designed to overflow at times of heavy rain, running into storm water drains that discharge directly into the ocean or waterways.
“So we get sewage contamination into the storm water and therefore on to the beaches,” Khan said.
Because Coogee beach was a very steep catchment, “when it rains, you very quickly generate a lot of runoff moving … into the storm water system, and very quickly down to the beach”, he said.
As a semi-protected bay, Coogee “doesn’t flush as well as some of the other beaches”.

“After a big wet weather event, you can see the water in Coogee turn brown and stay that way for potentially a couple of days,” Khan said. “So you’re more likely to take a sample that’s contaminated at Coogee than you might at Bondi, even if you had the same pollution going on, because Bondi will flush out quicker and recover quicker with clean marine water.”

Khan, who also chaired a NSW Environment Protection Authority expert panel to investigate the poo balls that washed up on Sydney beaches, said wastewater outflows from the Malabar waste treatment plant were a “negligible contributor” to Coogee’s poor water quality, as those deep ocean discharges occurred kilometres out to sea.
after newsletter promotion

Across all NSW swimming sites, including rivers, lagoons and tidal pools, 79% were rated “good” or “very good”, which the government characterised as a statewide improvement “largely associated with drier weather conditions across many parts of NSW during the reporting period, which generally reduced stormwater runoff and pollution entering waterways”.
Twelve other Sydney swimming spots received a rating of “poor” – including the Bayview baths, Frenchmans bay, the Kyeemagh baths and Rose Bay beach, which are all classified as estuarine sites.
Foreshores beach, beside Sydney airport, and the Gymea Bay baths were the only two Sydney sites to receive ratings of “very poor”, in addition to Yosemite Creek in the Blue Mountains.
The government advises swimming should always be avoided at “very poor” sites, while the water quality at “poor” sites is often unsuitable, especially after rain.
Malabar beach in the Randwick local government area, and Shelly beach in Manly, which both received a rating of “poor” last year, improved to a “good” rating this year.

blocks.caption: One Mile beach in the Port Stephens area received one of the highest water quality rankings in NSW.  Photograph: Jarryd Salem

blocks.text: Eight coastal beaches shared the state’s highest water quality rankings, including Avalon beach in Sydney’s north, Wollongong’s City beach, One Mile beach in the Hunter, and three Central Coast beaches.

“Good environmental decisions rely on good science,” the NSW environment minister, Penny Sharpe, said. “Through decades of consistent monitoring, Beachwatch provides the robust data needed to track water quality trends and give swimmers confidence in the information they use.”

articles.title: DoJ backs Trump ban on CNN, Politico and MS Now, citing security concerns
articles.summary: The news organizations, which sued the US president, are claiming the ban violates the first amendment

blocks.text: The US Department of Justicehas defended Donald Trump’s decision to ban three new organizations from the White House in a court filing, arguing that access to the grounds was a “privilege” and citing national security concerns.

Lawyers for the US president doubled down on Trump’s claims about CNN, Politico and MS Now reporting “Fake News” and insisted the ban did not violate the first amendment because “access to the White House is a privilege, not a right”.

In the court filing, justice department lawyers argued that Trump had concluded the news outlets “fail to satisfy the minimum requirements of professionalism” by relying on anonymous sources, and not giving the White House enough time to comment.
Trump’s lawyers also claimed the three organizations had violated “decorum” by publishing classified or sensitive national security information.
The justice department asked Timothy Kelly, the federal judge overseeing the case, to allow Trump to enforce his White House ban on reporters from CNN, Politico and MS Now.
The judge is expected to hold a hearing on the new organizations’ request for a temporary restraining order on Wednesday at 3.30 pm ET.

CNN, Politico and MS Now sued Trump on Monday, days after the president announced he would institute a White House ban on all three for reporting “fake news” – an accusation the US president has repeatedly made against media outlets, often without citing evidence.
The three news organizations are asking judge Kelly to stop Trump from enforcing his ban and to restore their hard passes to the White House, claiming the ban violates the first amendment.
But Trump and his justice department insist the ban does not infringe on the right to the free press; rather, it addresses “national security” threats.

In Tuesday’s filing, lawyers for the justice department said it sent letters to CNN, Politico and MS Now on 22 September outlining examples of reports that violated “the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex”.
The letters cited various “reporting incidents”, including some that “threatened national security and spread falsehoods”.

That includes CNN’s reporting on construction of the East Wing bunker under the White House ballroom; MS Now’s reporting on an alleged leak investigation; and Politico’s reporting on how the US Secret Service would invest money into security improvements for Trump’s ballroom.

articles.title: ‘Watermelons’: Zack Polanski and the rise of the ‘green outside, red inside’ eco-populists
articles.summary:
Author Russell Warfield argues the Green leader’s brand of politics is not new but has evolved in the party over time

Watermelons: the term used to describe the members of the Green party…

blocks.text: Watermelons: the term used to describe the members of the Green party of England and Wales who are green on the outside and red on the inside. People in this faction are environmentalists but bleed socialist ideologies.

Of the roughly 160,000 people who have flocked to the party since Zack Polanski became leader last year, most are thought to be in this camp, drawn to a political space on the left that they see as vacated by the Labour party.

But the author of a new book – The Green Socialist: Zack Polanski and the Battle for Britain’s Future – says this flavour of Green is nothing new. “What you’ve got to understand is that the party has been watermelon for at least 10 years,” says Russell Warfield, a former party staffer who has worked on election campaigns, including Polanski’s.

“There’s often this dichotomy presented that there’s this ‘real core’ Green party who are these ecologists who really just care about conservation of the environment, then there’s this new cohort of hard leftists,” Warfield says. “Actually, this has been both an organic process but also one which reaches much more deeply into the past of the party, where a lot of the fundamental positions of the party can be traced back to the early 1970s.”

His book unpacks the history of the party to explain how Polanski fits into it, arguing that the leader and his “eco-populist” package is not a departure from Green tradition but the culmination of a 50-year evolution that has turned the party into the main electoral force on the British left.

Not everyone agrees. During the leadership contest between Polanski and co-runners Adrian Ramsay and Ellie Chowns in 2025, a senior Green source described Polanski’s rise as a “hostile takeover”. Even Caroline Lucas, the Greens’ first MP and a former party leader, has said, when pressed, that she would love him to talk about the environment more.
“It’s just obvious nonsense,” Warfield says of the hostile takeover comment. “Look at the mandate, it was 85%,” Polanski’s landslide leadership win. “He won across every wing of the party.”

blocks.caption: Russell Warfield. Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian

blocks.text: But how green are the Greens? Since Polanski took over, he has been splashed across newspapers and TV screens discussing subjects ranging from Gaza to wealth taxes – progressive politics, but not necessarily or overtly green.

Warfield responds with a statistic: 34% of voters trust the Greens more than any other party on the environment, according to YouGov polling – the highest level of trust recorded for any party on any issue. “There is not a voter in this country, leftwing, rightwing, old, young, rural, urban, whatever, that does not strongly associate the Green party with taking action on the environment.”

Because of that starting point, he argues, the sensible move forward was to evolve into a broader message – one previous leaders paved the way for. “The reason the party exists is in recognition of the fact that just having a bunch of environmental conservation movements isn’t addressing the root political and economic causes of environmental degradation.

“We tried 50 years of that. And it got us so far, but the manifest moments of material advancement have been tied to moments where we’ve been able to be more responsive to the actual political context of the day.”

Warfield points out that many of Polanski’s positions are not his alone. Green party members vote on policy and the leaders are constitutionally duty bound to advocate for it. “Take the wealth tax,” Warfield writes. “He did not arrive at this policy personally. A ‘wealth tax’ is called for as ‘a means of limiting large accumulations of wealth’ in a Green party manifesto published long before Polanski’s leadership.”

The book finds links between the party’s past and present, even in unlikely places. It’s unavoidable, Warfield writes, that there were “some distinctly rightwing people present at the formation of the Green party”. The first key figure was Teddy Goldsmith, an environmentalist part of a famous Tory family. His writings formed key texts for People, the political party from which the modern Greens descend.
after newsletter promotion

But even Goldsmith – whose “deep ecology” philosophy leaned into Malthusian concerns about human population and misanthropic views that blamed humanity as a monolith for ecological degradation – shares threads with Polanski’s Greens, Warfield says. Both share the golden Green rule that infinite economic growth and endless extraction are impossible on a planet with finite resources. Both reject the idea that capitalism can simply carry on with business as usual, green or otherwise.

As the party has shifted towards social ecology over the years, Warfield says Polanski’s eco-socialism simply represents a modern evolution: arguing that capitalism and the 1% – not all of humanity – are the root cause of environmental destruction.

But Polanski’s tenure has also brought controversies. There was his criticism of the police response to the Golders Green attack, which the Met commissioner, Mark Rowley, called “inaccurate and misinformed”. There was the false claim he was a British Red Cross spokesperson and the sharing of a photo of a man with a T-shirt showing a guillotine and the phrase “we’re only making plans for Nigel”, a reference to Nigel Farage. YouGov polling shows Polanski’s approval rating has slumped since he became leader, while Green voting intention has dropped from 21% of the electorate in March to 11% this month.

Should the party take Polanski’s social media away? “Golders Green was a misstep,” says Warfield. “But what you don’t want to do is to get to a situation where every post needs double-tick signoff from different members of staff and you can’t just let Zack engage with social media in the way that allows him to reap the political points of authenticity.”

Polanski was criticised for his refusal to apologise for sharing the Farage guillotine picture. “Reform were trying to goad him into apologising for incitement to murder,” Warfield says. “If you do that, you legitimise the claim that they’re making. I think there’s a lot of strength in not succumbing to the pressure of playing that game.”

On 8 October, Polanski will contest the Holborn and St Pancras byelection after Keir Starmer announced his decision to vacate the seat. Warfield thinks Polanski can win. “You could vote Labour again and you get another backbencher who is one among literally hundreds of Labour MPs and that doesn’t make much difference to anything,” he says. “Or you can put a really prominent, independently minded Green in there and continue to put pressure on the Burnham project from its left.”

articles.title: Pakistan's jailed former PM Khan's sons told DW the authorities are cracking down ahead of new PTI protests
articles.summary: The sons of jailed Pakistani ex-PM Imran Khan told DW their father is in ill-health while being isolated from family and doctors. Other family members have been detained ahead of a planned opposition…

image.caption: Despite being jailed since 2022, Khan remains a popular political figure in PakistanImage: K.M. Chaudhry/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Family members of Pakistan's former Prime Minister Imran Khan are concerned about the 73-year-old's health in a Rawalpindi prison, accusing authorities of preventing him from accessing appropriate medical care.
Khan's London-based sons, Sulaiman and Kasim Khan, told DW they have received "little to no information" about their father's health condition.
"When we last spoke to him on the phone back in March, he said that he had lost 85% of the vision in his right eye and that despite his complaints, it was neglected for months," they said.

The brothers added that their father was being held in a tiny cell and has been allowed outside for only one or two hours a day. They also allege that the elder Khan was kept in isolation from family, lawyers, and a personal physician for 10 months before he was briefly allowed to see two of his sisters.
This comes amid the opposition Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party's planned protest march on September 27 to exert pressure on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's government for Khan's release.
Sons demand family access and medical care for Khan
Khan's sons are urging authorities to allow their father to receive an independent medical assessment and restore regular access to his family and medical team.

"We are asking the Pakistani authorities to obey the Supreme Court orders immediately and shift our father to Shifa International Hospital so that he can be assessed by independent doctors," they said.
They also called for Khan to be allowed his mandated family visits, phone calls with his sons, and access to a personal physician.

blocks.caption: Pro-Khan protesters clashed with authorities during a 2024 protestImage: ASIF HASSAN/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Khan's sisters detained as PTI plans new protests

Despite being in jail, Khan remains at the center of Pakistan's political confrontation between the PTI and the country's powerful military. He also remains a popular political figure in Pakistan, despite being ousted from office in 2022 in a parliamentary no-confidence vote.
Amid plans for a PTI protest march set for this weekend, Khan's three sisters were detained in the Punjab capital of Lahore on Monday.
The detention orders cited concerns that the sisters were a threat to public safety and maintenance of public order. All three were ordered to be held for 30 days under a public order ordinance.
Khan's sons told DW the arrests were intended to intimidate their family and supporters before the planned protest rally.

"Our family members who have been arbitrarily taken into custody must be released immediately," they said. "The abductions of our family members in the middle of the night, with no reason given, were purely to intimidate them," they added.

Khan was ousted as prime minister in 2022 and jailed the following year on what he says are politically motivated corruption charges. Khan's family members, and his PTI opposition party, have faced an ongoing government crackdown.

blocks.caption: The detention orders for Khan's sisters cited concerns that they were a threat to public safety and maintenance of public orderImage: AAMIR QURESHI/AFP

blocks.text: Pakistan government calls for 'order'
Pakistan's government has rejected the PTI's characterization of the crackdown and says its priority is to maintain public order during the planned protest.
Talal Chaudhary, Pakistan's minister of state for interior, has warned that the government will not tolerate unlawful activity or actions threatening lives and property.
"If you are a peaceful citizen, come to Islamabad from any route, come 100 times," Chaudhary told DW.
"But if you come as terrorists, we will not let you leave," he added.

In 2024, pro-Khan protests on the streets of Islamabad turned violent. Demonstrators breached high security zones and clashes with security forces, leaving six dead. When Khan was first arrested in May 2023, nationwide PTI support rallies also led to violence, with military and government buildings suffering damage. Several people were killed and hundreds injured.
Chaudhary said the government would not tolerate unlawful activity or actions threatening lives and property.
"The right to protest does not give the right to attack," he said.

Authorities have stepped up security preparations in Islamabad and Rawalpindi ahead of the protest, including the deployment of thousands of police personnel and the placement of shipping containers and other barriers at key entry points.
Can Pakistan still help end the US-Iran war?
Arrests could 'galvanize' PTI supporters
The PTI has said the September 27 protest will demand Khan's release and push for what the opposition describes as respect for constitutional and political rights.

Michael Kugelman, a South Asia analyst at the Washington-based Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars, told DW the arrests will likely further energize Khan's supporters ahead of the planned protest.
"The arrests will galvanize what is already an angry and anxious Khan support base," Kugelman said.

The detention of Khan's sisters, who Kugelman said are "prominent advocates" of Khan's cause, has also placed his family increasingly at the center of the confrontation between the government and the PTI.
Khan's base is "concerned about the state of his health, and for his sister to be detained will increase the chance that protesters take to the streets on the 27th," he added.
Zulfi Bukhari, a senior PTI leader and close aide to Khan, said the arrests were meant to create fear but will not prevent the party from mobilizing its supporters across the country.
"What they don't realize is all they are doing is creating more hatred for themselves among the public," Bukhari told DW, referring to the government.
Bukhari described the current crackdown as the most severe the PTI has faced. "This crackdown seems the more brutal," he said, adding that the government was acting out of frustration.

"They are fueling a fire that will soon be out of their control," asserted Bukhari. "They can keep attacking us, and we will continue to resist. This protest will go on, and many more after it," he added.

As Pakistan's government is dealing with several challenges, including economic malaise, conflict with the Afghan Taliban, and fallout from the Iran war, further domestic unrest would be an unwelcome complication.
Pakistan: 'Security state' on the rise amid regional tension
