articles.summary: Alex Eala is expected to draw a huge crowd in her round of 16 clash against Russia’s Tatiana Prozorova after her packed fan event at the Singapore Open

blocks.text: CROWD DARLING. The Philippines' Alex Eala takes a photo with fans after her Q&A session in the 2026 Singapore Open.
WTA/Ashok Kumar
Alex Eala is expected to draw a huge crowd in her round of 16 clash against Russia’s Tatiana Prozorova after her packed fan event at the Singapore Open

items: Filipina tennis star Alex Eala is receiving strong support at the Singapore Open, where she is set to compete against Russia's Tatiana Prozorova in the round of 16.
Eala, ranked No. 18, is a heavy favorite against Prozorova, who is ranked No. 180 and is making her debut in the round of 16 at a WTA 500 event.
Eala recently returned from the US Open and hopes to continue her success in Singapore, aiming for a quarterfinal match against either Xinyu Wang or Joanna Garland.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Alex Eala is thousands of kilometers away from home, but it does not feel that way for the Filipina tennis star as she enjoys fervent support when she opens her Singapore Open campaign.
Eala is expected to draw a huge crowd in her round of 16 clash against Russia’s Tatiana Prozorova at Centre Court of the OCBC Arena on Thursday, September 24, after her packed fan event.
Throngs of fans, including Singaporean locals, flocked to The Kallang on Wednesday, September 23, to catch a glimpse of Eala during her Q&A session — a testament to her growing star power.
And Eala hopes to repay their adoration as she looks to avoid the upset ax against Prozorova, who is ranked No. 180 in the world.

blocks.caption: SUPERSTAR. The Philippines’ Alex Eala during her Q&A session in the 2026 Singapore Open.

blocks.text: Sitting at a career-high No. 18 ranking, Eala earned a first-round bye as the third seed and will battle Prozorova coming off a much-needed break following her run to the third round in the US Open.

The WTA 500 event marks Eala’s first tournament in over two weeks after her US Open stint ended at the hands of good friend Iva Jovic — the Filipina even returning briefly to the Philippines before flying to Singapore.

Eala stands as the heavy favorite against the 22-year-old Russian, who only has one Grand Slam main draw appearance and is seeing action in the round of 16 of a WTA 500 event for the first time in her career.
Prozorova pulled off a 5-7, 7-6 (2), 6-2 win over Belgium’s Sofia Costoulas to achieve that feat.
If Eala gets past Prozorova, she will face the winner between China’s Xinyu Wang and Chinese Taipei’s Joanna Garland in the quarterfinals. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Slovakia: PM Robert Fico's NATO Article 5 remarks spark criticism and raise questions about his country's NATO commitment
articles.summary: Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico says he fears war and will do everything he can to keep his country out of one. Critics say his remarks risk weakening NATO, the alliance that was designed to…

image.caption: 'I do not want Slovakia to be part of any military conflict because of some Article 5,' said Slovak PM Robert FicoImage: Martin Baumann/TASR/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "I'm afraid of war," Robert Fico told medical students at a teaching hospital in Presov last week.

"What is happening in Europe today, what we're hearing and seeing today, is that the military conflict in Ukraine has got out of control," he went on, warning them that Europe faced the possibility of a wider war.

He asked the students to imagine Slovakia being told to prepare "5,000 soldiers, 10,000 soldiers" who would go somewhere to fight "without us even knowing whom they are fighting, or why, or what for."
Then he turned to Article 5 of NATO's founding treaty, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.
"I do not want Slovakia to be part of any military conflict because of some Article 5," Fico said.

"Yes, we are in NATO. We value that. Cooperation and fulfilling our obligations matter to us. But as prime minister, I will do everything to ensure that Slovakia is never drawn into a military conflict."

blocks.caption: Czech President Petr Pavel has questioned whether Fico understands the meaning of the word 'solidarity'Image: Metin Aktas/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

blocks.text: The remarks prompted uproar from the Slovak opposition and also a spat with Petr Pavel, president of neighboring Czechia and former chairman of NATO's Military Committee.
"If anyone says they're glad to be a member of NATO … but are unwilling to get involved if anyone else is attacked, then they have not understood the word solidarity," Pavel said.
Fico replied that he understood that Pavel, as a former NATO general, would like to fight, while he himself preferred peace.
The impact on Slovakia's standing
The Slovak prime minister's fear of a wider war is shared by many Europeans. But critics at home gave his remarks short shrift.

"Isn't he a prime minister? Isn't he the leader of a country? Is he not supposed to lead people instead of expressing fears?" asked former Slovak Foreign Minister Miro Wlachovsky, now a distinguished fellow at the GLOBSEC think tank.

blocks.caption: Slovak PM Robert Fico (left) and Czech PM Andrej Babis (right) have both stressed their preference for diplomacy when it comes to ending the war in Ukraine Image: Jaroslav Ozana/CTK/picture alliance

blocks.text: "My question for him as prime minister is: OK, even if the situation is as bad as you are saying, what I want to hear from you is how the country is prepared. What have you done for preparedness? Who will come to our aid in case we are attacked?" Wlachovsky told DW.
Asked whether Fico's remarks could damage Slovakia's standing among its allies, Wlachovsky replied: "It's already done."
Political background to Fico's comments
Analysts see a clear political context to Fico's remarks.

The Slovak prime minister will face a difficult reelection fight next year. Some observers believe Fico is trying to steal votes from the extreme-right Republika party, which is viscerally hostile to NATO and the EU and opposes military support for Ukraine.

Wlachovsky compared Fico's rhetoric to that of Hungary's former Prime Minister Viktor Orban and the current Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, both of whom have presented themselves as the candidates of peace.

Babis was heavily criticized during his unsuccessful 2023 presidential campaign after questioning during a televised debate whether the Czech Republic should send troops to NATO ally Poland if it came under attack.
What is NATO's Article 5?
Oana Lungescu, a distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute and a former NATO spokesperson, told DW that Article 5 was "the most solemn pledge that a country can make to another."
But its central purpose, she said, was deterrence: convincing a potential aggressor that it would face the alliance together, rather than an isolated member.
"This is about solidarity, standing together, underpinning deterrence and therefore avoiding war," she said. "NATO is a defensive alliance. It's not an offensive alliance."
Nor would invoking Article 5 automatically send every member's troops into combat, she said.

The North Atlantic Council, where every ally is represented, would assess an attack and decide by consensus whether it constituted an Article 5 situation — Slovakia's voice would be equal to that of its 31 partners in that room, she said.
Once consensus was reached, each country would then assist the attacked ally by taking the action it deemed necessary, which might — or might not — involve armed force.
Article 5 has been invoked only once, following the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States.
Lungescu pointed to one of NATO's initial responses: sending AWACS surveillance aircraft to patrol US skies and help prevent another attack.

blocks.caption: Solidarity: Slovakia's neighbors and NATO allies Poland and Czechia in 2022 pledged to protect Slovak airspace.Image: Petr David Josek/AP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: She pointed out that Slovakia already benefits from the same solidarity Fico appeared to question. The country hosts a NATO multinational battlegroup established after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with personnel from several allies alongside Slovak troops.
Its purpose is to deter an attack on Slovakia.
'Exactly what Putin wants'
For former Slovak Defense Minister Jaroslav Nad, the danger lies in allowing that fear to dictate policy towards Ukraine.
"This is exactly what Vladimir Putin wants," said Nad, who was defense minister from 2020 to 2023 and is now head of the non-parliamentary opposition Democrats party.

"He wants citizens in the EU and NATO to believe that if EU and NATO countries continue to support Ukraine, this escalatory situation might lead to a Third World War or something like that," Nad told DW.

Nad was in office when Slovakia decided to hand over its entire fleet of ageing MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine. Fico's government later sought a criminal investigation into the transfer; prosecutors closed the case, finding no crime.

"Even when I was defense minister, I heard this not only from ordinary people but also from some ministers around the table: that we shouldn't help Ukraine with this or that equipment or capability or ammunition, because it might create a difficult situation in terms of escalation towards Russia," he went on.
"None of that happened."
Could Slovakia replace Hungary as EU's main disruptor?

articles.title: Germany's oldest party, the center-left SPD, is in a difficult position following its success in the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state election
articles.summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) has vowed to press ahead with controversial reforms, but resistance is mounting within his coalition partner, the SPD. How much dissent can a governing coalition…

image.caption: Manuela Schwesig is the new center of power in the SPDImage: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: Following state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, two of Germany's 16 federal states, the mood within the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) is oscillating between relief and frustration, confidence and bewilderment. "The SPD is clearly capable of winning more than 30% of the vote," party co-leader Lars Klingbeil said jubilantly in Berlin. "This result in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is an encouragement for the entire Social Democratic movement."

As Klingbeil put it, Manuela Schwesig, the SPD state premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and her party had shown "how to make up ground, how to fight, and how, with the right issues and the right approach, to stage a comeback and ultimately win people over through that effort."

What Klingbeil conveniently omits is that Schwesig's success was also due to the fact that she distanced herself as much as possible from the federal government's policies, and by extension from the SPD at the national level, which it governs in coalition with the center-right CDU/CSU alliance of the Christian Democratic Union and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union under Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The national government has meanwhile become more unpopular than any of its predecessors.
Me or the AfD: SPD state premier presents a stark choice
Focus on the SPD's traditional values

Schwesig scored points above all with her opposition to parts of the federal government's pension reform plans. At the post-election review meeting in Berlin, she intensified her criticism, launching a pointed attack on the chancellor. She argued that 81% of people in her state consider the reforms unfair and that Merz is misjudging the situation.

On election night, Friedrich Merz made clear that he was all the more determined to stay the course. "The reforms must go ahead," the chancellor said. "Of course, this puts all of us in a difficult position. What needs to be done now requires courage, resilience, and patience. I will demonstrate those qualities as leader of the CDU and, above all, as chancellor of our country."

Schwesig had a clear response. "My advice to the chancellor, if he wants to regain people's trust, though I'm not sure that's still possible, is that he needs to engage with the reality on the ground." She argued that Merz must ask himself what needs to change. "There can be no business as usual."
What are the German government's pension, labor reforms?
Bas and Klingbeil struggle to chart a course

The SPD, and above all its leaders, Lars Klingbeil and Bärbel Bas, now find themselves in a dilemma. Both serve as cabinet ministers in Merz's government and therefore help implement policies that many SPD members are increasingly questioning.

At the same time, they are accountable to their party and must ensure that SPD priorities are reflected in government policy. The success Schwesig achieved with her unequivocally critical stance is now putting them under considerable pressure.
Following her electoral victory, Schwesig has emerged as one of the most influential figures within the SPD. Many party members would like to see Schwesig become the party's next leader.

She already seemed to be stepping into that role as she stood before the microphone at the post-election review, dressed entirely in red and projecting confidence. By contrast, Bas and Klingbeil appeared almost defensive, seeking to strike a balance between criticizing the coalition and supporting it.

"If people in our country perceive reforms as something that threatens their way of life and leads only to things getting worse, then it is not just our communication that needs to improve. In some areas, the substance of the reforms themselves needs to change as well," said Klingbeil.
Bas called for both a "reality check" and a "fairness check" on the reforms, arguing that they must be workable in practice and socially equitable.
Show confidence, uphold socialdemocratic values

Will that be enough? Calls for the SPD to be "more like Schwesig", in other words, to assert its own positions with greater confidence, are growing ever louder within the party. The only question is how much dissent a governing party can afford to show. "Nothing would be more damaging than allowing this coalition to collapse over a policy dispute at this point," Bas warned. Solutions, she argued, "are possible within this coalition as well."

At a leadership committee meeting on the morning after the state elections, the SPD leadership adopted a strategy paper. Across nine key points, it sets out the priorities the party intends to champion in government. One section is headed "Real Change Instead of Simply Cutting Spending", while another is titled "An Affordable Life for All".

The SPD wants inheritance tax reform to ensure that the resulting revenue can fund a "genuine education initiative". On pension reform, the paper states that important questions remain unresolved regarding phased retirement and the right to retire without pension reductions after 45 years of contributions.
The SPD therefore makes its position clear: "The lifetime achievements of people who have paid into the system for many years must continue to make a difference."

It remains unclear whether the CDU/CSU will respond to these demands. The same is true of the simmering debate over whether Bas and Klingbeil should be replaced at the helm of the party. Pressure continues to come from Philipp Türmer, leader of Jusos, the SPD's youth wing. "I'm not saying that the two of them are the problem, but at the moment they're not part of the solution either," he told German broadcaster RTL and its news channel ntv.

Türmer and others had called for a special party conference that could have paved the way for replacing Bas and Klingbeil. Instead, the party will hold only a convention in December, a smaller party gathering that cannot elect or remove party leaders. From now on, however, SPD members are likely to judge their leaders even more by how effectively they defend the SPD's positions in government and whether they can restore the party's appeal among voters.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: New powerful synthetic opioid behind sharp rise in Scottish drugs deaths
articles.summary:
Eleven per cent increase in fatalities last year partly down to presence of nitazenes in Scotland’s illicit drug market

A new type of powerful synthetic opioid have contributed to a sharp…

blocks.text: New forms of a powerful synthetic opioid have contributed to a sharp rise in Scottish drug deaths, with the latest data showing an 11% increase in fatalities last year

Annual figures released by National Records of Scotland (NRS) on Wednesday recorded 1,133 drug-related deaths in 2025, 116 more than the previous year. The 2025 figures are the sixth highest on record.

Opiates and opioids, which include drugs such as heroin, remain the most deadly drug types, implicated in 78% of all deaths. But the presence of nitazenes – a highly potent type of synthetic opioid – rose by more than 200%, from 76 deaths in 2024 to 247 in 2025.

Maree Todd, the minister for mental wellbeing, public health, sport, alcohol and drugs, said an “increasingly toxic and unpredictable drugs supply” required “more coordinated action across the country”.

Last year’s data showed a decrease in Scotland’s drug deaths for the first time since 2017, but the charity Scottish Drugs Forum (SDF) warned at the time that this was most likely a blip, masking a recent surge in synthetic opioids in Scotland’s illicit drug market.

blocks.caption: Nitazenes are created in laboratories and can be hundreds of times stronger than traditional opiates and opioids. Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images

blocks.text: Unlike plant-derived drugs such as heroin, nitazenes are created in illegal laboratories and can be hundreds of times stronger than traditional opiates and opioids. They are also often mixed with other drugs, increasing the risks to users who do not always know what is present in the supply.

SDF’s chief executive, Kirsten Horsburgh, said the increase in drug deaths reflected a range of factors “including an increasingly unpredictable drugs supply”. The increased presence of nitazenes was “a stark indication of [the] changing risks”, she added

Horsburgh said: “It is too simplistic to say that 1,133 people died because of the contaminated drug supply, or indeed because of drug use itself. The truth is that these deaths are shaped by a much wider set of factors, including poverty, trauma, deprivation, housing insecurity and mental health inequality.”
The figures showed drug-related deaths were 15 times higher in Scotland’s most deprived areas than in the least deprived. There was a 19% rise in deaths among men, withthe average age of death 46.

Todd said the government had funded more than 1,100 residential rehabilitation placements last year and widened access to treatment. But, she added, “despite these policy interventions, and the actions of our valued frontline workers, it is clear we need to do much more to reduce this tragic loss of life”.
The new figures mean Scotland remains Europe’s “drug deaths capital”, with the worst fatality rate in the continent.

Before the figures were published, the Scottish government announced that a new drug-checking service, which will allow users to submit drugs for rapid testing and provide harm reduction advice, would open early next month in Glasgow’s safer drug consumption facility. Similar drug-checking services have been approved in Aberdeen and Dundee, with a fourth expected in Edinburgh.

articles.title: Discord, Reddit given more time to establish Philippine offices, says CICC
articles.summary: The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) on Wednesday said that it gave Reddit and Discord more time to put up their respective offices in the Philippines after the platforms…

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 9:12pm

The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) on Wednesday said that it gave Reddit and Discord more time to put up their respective offices in the Philippines after the platforms expressed their willingness to work with the government in addressing online threats.

The CICC on Tuesday gave both platforms 24 hours to establish a Philippine presence within 24 hours to enhance collaboration with the government following the shooting at the Banga National High School in South Cotabato.
Reddit said that it would establish an office in the Philippines, while Discord reached out to say that it was willing to work with the CICC to address the issue.

“We decided to grant them an extension since they responded within the 24 hours, and we want to give them the opportunity to work with us because what we want is accountability and a clear mechanism for government to coordinate with the platforms,” CICC Executive Director Undersecretary Renato “Aboy” Paraiso said in a statement.

“While we welcome their commitment to work with us, we will not settle for anything less. This commitment must translate into concrete action, genuine accountability, faster response mechanisms and stronger protections for our Filipino children online,” he added.

The online meeting was attended by Reddit Vice President of Policy Jessica Ashooh, Deputy General Counsel Leslie Liu and Policy and Regulatory Affairs Manager Vijay Pamarathi. They discussed establishing “green lanes” or direct lines with Philippine authorities wherein the latter could flag potentially harmful content.
This would also involve online sexual abuse and exploitation of children (OSAEC), child abuse and exploitation materials (CSAEM), and Nihilistic Violent Extremism (NVE).
Discord told the CICC that the newly rolled out Global Teen Experience would ensure that teenagers are placed in age-appropriate places on their platform.

Discord Senior Public Policy Advisor Vasundhara Singh said that users who cannot be placed in a specific age group will have to confirm their age through facial age estimation, with biometric data not being stored in Discord.

The shooting in South Cotabato is the third school shooting incident in 2026. In June, two students opened fire in a high school in Tacloban, killing three others. Not more than two months later, in August, another student shot and killed a schoolmate in Ateneo de Zamboanga before turning the gun on himself. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Canada’s Mexico visa requirements limit country’s tourism potential, says tour operator
articles.summary: The Canadian government sees Mexico as a growing market for tourism and projects visits to rise by 40 per cent over the next four years, hitting nearly half a million visitors spending about $1…

image.caption: Jesus Martinez, left, general manager of Dream Destinations Mexico, meets with Tobias Barth, who co-owns Whitehorse’s Northern Lights Resort and Spa, during a business-to-business 'speed-dating' event in Mexico City on Sept. 22, 2026. (Tania Miranda Perez/CBC)

blocks.text: World·New

The Canadian government sees Mexico as a growing market for tourism and projects visits to rise by 40 per cent over the next four years, hitting nearly half a million visitors spending about $1 billion a year by 2030.
Federal agency hosted business-to-business encounters between tour operators in Mexico City
The visa requirements Canada has imposed on Mexicans limit the full market potential the country offers as a source of tourists, according to a Mexican tour operator.

While the number of Mexicans visiting Canada is growing, the visa requirements reimposed in the late winter of 2024 had an immediate impact on the figures, said Jesus Martinez, general manager of Dream Destinations Mexico.
"We haven’t recovered the numbers that we would love, but the numbers are going up," said Martinez in an interview with CBC News.
He said scrapping the visa is on his "wish list," but he isn’t holding his breath waiting for the change.
"It’s not up to us," said Sanchez, whose company builds tour packages it sells to agencies and individuals.
The government under prime minister Justin Trudeau initially lifted the visa requirement for Mexicans travelling to Canada in 2016. His government then reimposed the requirement, under U.S. pressure.
Mexicans are eligible to enter Canada by air under an Electronic Travel Authorization if they hold a valid, non-immigrant U.S. visa or have held a Canadian visa in the past 10 years.
'Untapped' potential

Martinez was attending a type of speed-dating event this week for Canadian and Mexican tour operators at a Mexico City hotel hosted by Destination Canada, the federal Crown corporation responsible for promoting Canadian tourism.
Canadian and Mexican tour operators participated in 12-minute rounds of one-on-one meetings to build ties and business opportunities.

items: U.S. may seek win with Mexico in wake of collapsed trade talks with Canada, says ex-negotiator
Alberta beef entering Mexico’s Costco market where U.S. cuts once reigned

blocks.text: During one of the rounds, Martinez sat down with Tobias Barth, who co-owns Whitehorse’s Northern Lights Resort and Spa.
"If we think about the aurora [borealis] viewing, how does that work on a day-to-day visit?" said Sanchez.

"That’s a really good question," said Barth. "The big benefit of being at Northern Lights Resort and Spa in the Yukon is that you don’t have to go anywhere … [Tourists] can see the northern lights right out of bed."
Barth told CBC News that Mexico is currently the resort’s fourth-largest source country for customers, behind U.S., domestic and Australian visitors.
Darlene Fedoroshyn, executive director of international marketing with Travel Alberta, said Mexico is a potential source of one million visitors a year for the province.
"The potential is pretty untapped at the moment," said Fedoroshyn. "The numbers are staggering, and so what we have to do is try to convert that."
Fedoroshyn acknowledged that the visa requirement could be a stumbling block for some Mexicans seeking to visit Canada.

"We always want to advocate for making it easier to come into Canada and we would work really hard with our federal government and with our [provincial] government to try to make it simpler for travellers," she said.
Mexican visitors at pre-pandemic levels

Canadian federal Tourism Minister Rechie Valdez attended the Destination Canada event. Valdez, who is also minister of women and gender equality, was scheduled to meet with Mexico’s secretary of tourism on Wednesday.
Valdez sidestepped CBC's questions on whether Canada would consider rescinding the visa requirement for Mexican visitors.

She said Canada is now seeing pre-pandemic levels of Mexican tourists and that the numbers continue to grow. Valdez said she would share any feedback she receives during her time in Mexico with her cabinet colleagues when she returns to Ottawa.
"It’s really important for us to ensure that we are doing everything we can to promote the growth and strength of our tourism sector," she said.

articles.title: Delays in Covid shots for kids is latest bid by Trump officials to restrict vaccines
articles.summary:
Administration is holding back Covid vaccines for all children in at least 11 states and one US territory

The Trump administration is holding back Covid vaccines for all children in at least…

blocks.text: The Trump administration is holding back Covid vaccines for all children in at least 11 states and one US territory, and officials have not indicated when or whether the shots will become available.
It’s the latest step by top officials to restrict vaccines in America – and it sets a precedent for holding back other immunizations, experts said.

“They’re using every means possible to try and make it harder to get vaccinated,” said Daniel Jernigan, the former director of the National Center for Emerging and Zoonotic Infectious Diseases at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

These actions could be a way of “testing the waters” on halting other vaccines in the federal Vaccines for Children (VFC) program, Jernigan said. “There’s nothing preventing them from doing that for the other vaccines as well,” he added.

More than half of children in the US receive vaccines through VFC, and some states and American Samoa are also known as “universal” vaccine purchasers, which means they buy vaccines through this system for all children in the state or territory, regardless of their insurance status or ability to pay. But as updated pediatric Covid shots roll out throughout the country amid a Covid wave, HHS is not providing Covid vaccines through the VFC program, with no timeline on when the vaccines will be sent.

That means the 52% of children who are eligible for VFC – because they are Alaska Native or American Indian, under- or uninsured, or enrolled in or eligible for Medicaid – as well as all children in universal VFC states don’t have access to Covid vaccines.

“The delay in VFC means delays in these states’ ability to get vaccine for all children,” said Demetre Daskalakis, former director of the CDC’s National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases and chief medical officer at Callen-Lorde Community health center.

The states with universal purchase programs include Alaska, Connecticut, Hawaii, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington, and Wyoming. Some states, like Idaho, also purchase some of the recommended vaccines in this way.

Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), confirmed that Covid vaccines are not available through VFC. Because Covid can circulate at other times as well, including in the summer, “an arbitrary September date should not be treated as a public-health deadline for Covid-19 vaccine procurement”.
The CDC is “finalizing decisions” about Covid vaccine procurement through the Vaccines for Children and Section 317 programs, and “additional information will be available soon,” Hilliard said.
She did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about the effects on universal VFC states.

The updated Covid shot provides the best protection against variants that are circulating now, Jernigan said. “Getting the updated vaccine out there is going to provide the most protection to kids,” he said. HHS is “not allowing the best vaccine to be out there to prevent the most disease.” Previous vaccines expired earlier this year.

Vaccinating children is especially important early in life; infants have one of the highest hospitalization rates from Covid after the 65-plus age group. “Those are kids that have never been exposed to Covid,” he said, and vaccination can help prevent these severe outcomes.
“It’s, in a sense, almost derelict that you would not make it available to those most vulnerable to severe disease,” Jernigan said.

Jernigan is concerned about the vaccines that were recently designated “shared clinical-decision making,” including hepatitis B, meningococcal vaccines, and the flu shot; a judge’s order has stayed such change for now.

Robert F Kennedy Jr, HHS secretary and longtime vaccine opponent, has claimed that these changes have not affected vaccination, even as public confidence in vaccines sags after years of misinformation.
“We have not taken vaccines away from anyone. We have preserved access,” he said at an anti-vaccine conference last week.
Hilliard, the HHS spokesperson, did not respond to a question about how Kennedy’s statement squared with the decision not to make Covid vaccines available.
“Not allowing universal ordering states to order vaccine is limiting access,” Daskalakis said.

The restrictions on vaccines are part of a pattern at HHS, Jernigan said, “trying to find each lever to keep the vaccine from being accessible.” The administration has taken multiple steps to decrease the availability of vaccines, “just making it harder and harder” to get the vaccines, he said, calling it “death by a thousand cuts”.

articles.title: Venezuela’s Delcy Rodríguez hails ‘historic meeting’ with Donald Trump in New York
articles.summary:
Interim president, who agreed a 65bn-barrel oil deal with the US, did not say whether she would visit her snatched predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, in jail

Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy…

blocks.text: Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, has celebrated a “historic” meeting with Donald Trump in New York, posing for a smiley photo with the US president less than nine months after he ordered the abduction of her boss, Nicolás Maduro.

The former foes met at a five-star hotel in Manhattan a few blocks from Trump Tower late on Tuesday, on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly. The hotel is about 7 miles from the Brooklyn prison where Maduro has been held since he was snatched during a special forces raid on Caracas.
On the eve of Tuesday’s encounter, an American reporter asked Rodríguez if she would be visiting Maduro, under whom she served as vice-president, during her stay in New York. She did not reply.

But Venezuela’s interim leader did find time to meet Trump at the luxury Lotte New York Palace hotel, with the get-together seen as a key part of Rodríguez’s push for international legitimacy after years of diplomatic isolation under Maduro’s dictatorship. On Wednesday she is expected to address the annual UN assembly.

“We held a historic meeting with … Donald Trump, with whom we discussed strengthening the bilateral relationship between our countries and advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, security and other matters of common interest,” Rodríguez wrote on Instagram, in a 133-word statement that made no mention of her incarcerated ally.

Oliver Blanco, one of Rodríguez’s top diplomats, claimed the meeting marked “a new stage of dialogue and understanding between both countries” and was “an important step toward new opportunities for our country and our people”. Blanco also posted a cheery photo in which both he and Trump smiled and gave the thumbs up to the camera.
A White House aide said the meeting was also attended by top US officials including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and the deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller.

Hours earlier, Rodríguez had sat in the general assembly hall watching Trump celebrate the “massive military operation” during which Maduro – whom he called an “outlaw dictator” and “a real criminal” – was captured. “It was a war … [and] to the victor belong the spoils,” Trump bragged of the recent oil deal between the US and Venezuela, as she appeared to wince.

Some observers also detected signs of discomfort in the body language captured in the photo of Trump and Rodríguez, who appears to be clenching her left fist as she poses beside the grinning US president.
Some of Rodríguez’s critics in Venezuela called her treatment by Trump an unmitigated humiliation for a socialist party politician who has spent years railing against Yankee imperialism.

After Maduro’s capture, Trump warned that Rodríguez would “pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro” if she did not toe the US line. Since then, Rodríguez has made a series of major concessions, including ceding control of Venezuela’s oil revenues to Washington and agreeing to a controversial 65bn-barrel oil deal that Trump on Tuesday called “the largest oil deal in history”.
One opposition figure denounced the Rodríguez/Trump meeting as an encounter between a “shameless puppet and her unscrupulous puppeteer”.

blocks.caption: Observers suggested Delcy Rodríguez’s clenched left hand signified her discomfort around Donald Trump. Photograph: Venezuelan Presidency/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: But Rodríguez has succeeded in consolidating power, with Trump seemingly more focused on gaining access to Venezuela’s natural resources than pushing for a fresh presidential election that would move the South American country back towards democracy.

Trump has repeatedly praised Rodríguez’s “fantastic” and “terrific” leadership while sidelining her main rival, the opposition leader María Corina Machado. Machado, who left Venezuela late last year to receive her Nobel peace prize in Oslo, has been unable to return and is exiled in Panama. She reportedly made three attempts to return to Venezuela this week, but failed.

Before Tuesday’s tête-à-tête, the presidents of the US and Venezuela had last met in 2015, when Barack Obama and Maduro spoke briefly during a regional summit in Panama. In the decade that followed, Maduro became an international pariah as he led his country into economic chaos and increasingly authoritarian rule, and Venezuela was hit by punishing international sanctions.

At the 2015 summit, Obama conceded that the days in which “the US could meddle with impunity” in Latin America were over. But Trump has dramatically different ideas and has been forging ahead with attempts to reassert US dominance in a region it has long considered its back yard.

As well as capturing Venezuela’s government and trying to topple Cuba’s communist government by strangling its economy, Trump’s push for hegemony has also seen the US accused of trying to swing Brazil’s presidential election in favour of the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro through diplomatic and economic pressure.

Addressing the UN assembly on Tuesday, the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, hit back at such efforts, without directly citing the US. “We will not allow the enemies of democracy – internal or external – to attack the will of the people. Brazilian democracy belongs to the Brazilians,” said Lula who is facing a tough battle to win re-election in October’s vote.

“Brazil doesn’t fit into anyone’s back yard,” added Lula, who also called for fresh elections in Venezuela. He did not meet Rodríguez during her visit to New York but said the “people of Venezuela deserve to decide their own future”.

articles.title: Questions swirl as members of Belleville, Ont., synagogue return after shooting
articles.summary: Some members of the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., took their first steps into the building Tuesday since the fatal shootout nearby on Sunday night.

image.caption: Norm Weddum, president of the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., points at bullet holes in a synagogue window on Sept. 22, 2026 (Michael Cole/CBC)

blocks.text: Ottawa
Some members of the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., took their first steps into the building Tuesday since the fatal shootout nearby on Sunday night.
Its president says they want to celebrate officer injured by the gunman
"It's kind of eerie to first step back in here," said Norm Weddum, president of the synagogue.
"We're all kind of looking at the damage … it's kind of surreal."
Congregants gathered at the synagogue for Sunday's Yom Kippur services were forced to take cover on the floor around 7 p.m when a gunman fired at a police officer in an unmarked car outside.
Const. Jeff Smith suffered serious injuries during the shootout with the 29-year-old shooter, Sean Ward, and a second officer who joined the exchange, officials said in a Monday news conference.
Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU) said Tuesday Smith remains in stable condition and that Ward died Monday night.

items: Suspect in Belleville, Ont., shooting is dead, SIU says

blocks.text: Weddum said he counted two dozen bullet holes in the synagogue's street-facing stained-glass windows.
He added that while he is glad to be allowed back in, he fears Ward's death will leave the community looking for answers.
"I'm kind of sad he died because I really wanted to find out his motive.… The police would have eventually questioned him."
The investigation into Sunday's events is ongoing. It's unclear if the shooting was targeting Smith, Sons of Jacob or the city's Jewish community.

A spokesperson for the Department of National Defence said Tuesday that Ward joined the Canadian Armed Forces in July 2017, that he served as an infantry soldier with Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry and was a corporal when he was released in June 2022 without having been deployed.
Neighbours near Ward's home in neighbouring Quinte West said he mostly kept to himself.
Sheri Skanes said she sometimes saw him playing with a dog in the backyard.
"I just think it's horrendous," she said of the shooting. "It's really sad what's happened."
Kevin Burley said he didn't know the suspect personally, but did have two "confrontations" with him about speeding where he said Ward responded in a way that was "very aggressive."
Suspect in Belleville, Ont., shooting near synagogue dies in hospital
Seeing police cars parked in their neighbourhood and hearing about the gunfire has been "very difficult to deal with," said Burley.
"Thank God the police officer was there to save these people. In my opinion, he is a hero. I hope he has a speedy recovery."
Weddum said one of the first things members of the synagogue want to do is celebrate Smith once he's recovered.
The congregation of roughly 35 families is focusing on moving forward, with many feeling relief they can soon get back into the building and run programs and services, Weddum said.
Members still have to decide when to fully reopen and there are plans to eventually do a larger community gathering.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jenna Legge is a reporter with CBC in Ottawa. Before that, she worked as a journalist on Prince Edward Island, with earlier stints in Winnipeg and Toronto. She holds a master's degree in international journalism from City University of London, and also studied journalism, law and political science at Carleton University. articles.title: Zelenskyy to address UN, Rubio to meet Russian counterpart — but few breakthroughs expected
articles.summary: Russia pounded Kyiv with drone strikes on Wednesday, hitting railway infrastructure, warehouses and fuel stations, just hours before Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy addresses the United…

image.caption: Firefighters extinguish a fire at a burning building following a Russian drone strike in Kyiv on Wednesday. (Danylo Antoniuk/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Russia pounded Kyiv with drone strikes on Wednesday, hitting railway infrastructure, warehouses and fuel stations, just hours before Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy addresses the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
Kremlin rejects idea of summit with Trump, Putin, Zelenskyy

At least two people were killed and 22 were injured ​in the morning attack, according to city authorities, in one ​of the heaviest strikes since Russia began attacking Kyiv and nearby areas over the summer with faster and high-flying jet drones that are harder to intercept.

Zelenskyy met with U.S. President Donald Trump Tuesday on the UN sidelines, where they discussed a potential bilateral ceasefire on energy-related targets and asked for increased supplies of U.S. Patriot air defence missiles to defend against an expected Russian winter campaign against Ukraine's electricity infrastructure. No agreements were reached, he said.

Trump said last week that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to strike energy targets, but any semblance of a truce disappeared when petrol stations in Kyiv were struck the following day and Ukraine bombed a Russian oil refinery.

For his part, Zelenskyy has said ‌he was ready for "any format" of an energy ceasefire with Moscow, as long as Russia halted its own attacks on Ukraine's infrastructure — something he doubts the Kremlin will honour.
Trump urges pause on energy attacks after Ukraine, Russia trade strikes

The Kremlin cautioned on Wednesday ahead of a planned meeting in New York between U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov that there were still no grounds for Ukraine peace talks to take place.
"For now, there are no prerequisites for moving onto a peaceful negotiating track, although we, as the Russian side, remain open to peace talks," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

items: Trump and Zelenskyy discuss potential for energy truce in face of new wave of strikes on infrastructure

blocks.text: Peskov said Russian President Vladimir Putin stood ready to meet Trump one-on-one if both leaders deemed such a meeting necessary. But he made it clear that Russia's stance on the possibility of Putin and Zelenskyy meeting in person had not changed.

The Kremlin has said that Zelenskyy would need to come to Moscow for such a meeting having already taken decisions Russia has been pushing for — an idea that Kyiv has repeatedly dismissed as unacceptable, suggesting any talks could only be held in a neutral country.
Peskov also played down the idea of a trilateral summit with the three presidents.
"Generally speaking, in any other circumstances, it would be inappropriate to hold a summit meeting before the groundwork has been laid at expert level, as this would be a waste of time," he said.
LISTEN | Victor Jack, NATO reporter for Politico, on latest tensions:
Front Burner26:05Why Russia has Europe on edge
U.S. ponders diesel export ban
France's President Emmanuel Macron said Monday he had discussed with Trump initiatives aimed at securing a moratorium on attacks linked to the energy sector.

The French leader said helping Ukraine's energy system remained a priority as the war continued to affect security across Europe and he hoped progress could be made during the annual gathering of leaders at the United Nations.
While Trump has blamed the attacks for soaring diesel prices in the U.S., most economic experts believe the U.S.-initiated Iran war has been a bigger factor.

items: Ontario farmers raise issue of high diesel prices with politicians at plowing match
Sky-high crude and diesel prices are fuelling protests worldwide

blocks.text: Trump said Tuesday he backed the idea of a diesel export ban supported by some Republican legislators in agricultural states. But it's not unanimously supported by all Republican members of Congress and it puts the president at odds with his own energy officials, who warn it could raise fuel prices on the coasts and tighten supplies for European allies.
"If you start putting barriers ​on flows, pretty quickly you will reduce the production, and you'll have less supply. We need more supply, not less supply," U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said.

Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, said that a ban would be unlikely to lower petroleum prices and ⁠could lead to retaliatory measures by energy exporting countries, which states like California rely on for some of their energy.
In a Tuesday interview with Fox News, Rubio suggested there was another reason for the U.S. concern about the strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.

"The one thing we are concerned about, however, is that over the last few months, on a number of occasions, American-linked ships, American oil supplies have been targeted, probably not deliberately, but targeted nonetheless by Ukraine," said Rubio, not specifying which U.S. companies he was referring to.

items: Putin's ruling party romps to win in wartime Russian election

blocks.text: In Russia, the Economy Ministry expects the country to produce and export less natural gas this year than previously forecast, according to a draft government document seen by Reuters. Earlier this month, Reuters reported that Russia had also downgraded its 2026 oil output forecast to a 17-year low and revised the fuel export outlook for this year and next due to the war with Ukraine.

Natural gas production and export forecasts have been revised down against the background of ruptured economic and political ties with the West over the Ukraine war and the European Union's plans to stop all purchases of Russian gas from next year. Russia's gas exports to Europe tumbled 44 per cent last year to the lowest amount since the mid-1970s, according to Reuters calculations, following the closure of the Ukrainian transit route.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Two roads diverged in the Senate on Wednesday, September 23 — and the Villar siblings took different ones.

Senator-judge Mark Villar broke ranks with his sister, Senator-judge Camille Villar, and the Senate minority bloc in a surprise vote on two key motions during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

On Wednesday, the Senate impeachment court heard oral arguments from the defense and prosecution panels on the September 8 appeal of Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo seeking to overturn the July 6 ruling of impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero, which set the voting threshold for Duterte’s conviction to 16.
Tulfo also wanted the court to revisit the denominator for the voting threshold amid the absence of Senator-judges Loren Legarda, Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, Rodante Marcoleta, and Jinggoy Estrada.

Legarda remains on extended medical leave abroad, while Dela Rosa is in hiding due to an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court over alleged crimes against humanity stemming from the Duterte administration’s drug war.
Marcoleta and Estrada are detained over separate plunder charges.

But before the court proceeded with the voting, Senator-judge Alan Peter Cayetano — who also serves as the Senate minority leader — made a last-minute bid to defer the vote, arguing that the impeachment court had no authority to interpret the Constitution.

Members of the Senate minority bloc, including Camille, voted in favor of Cayetano, except Mark, who abstained. Thirteen senator-judges then moved to junk the appeal, paving the way for the subsequent voting on Tulfo’s motion.

Mark voted to approve Tulfo’s motion. He was also the sole member of the Senate minority bloc present during the voting. Other minority senators opted to boycott it and not participate in the afternoon proceedings.
Why was Mark voting differently?
For Senator-judge Imee Marcos, the older Villar’s recent graft complaints might be related to the voting decisions.

blocks.caption: A Villar split: Why is Mark Villar breaking ranks with sister Camille?

blocks.text: “Well, we are aware of what he is experiencing. So, let us see his decisions,” Marcos told reporters.
Pressed for details, she added: “We know what’s happening with the minority senators. We are all being attacked.”

The Office of the Ombudsman previously said graft complaints were now pending against members of the Villar family due to allegations related to their PrimeWater Infrastructure Corporation. This includes the senator-siblings, their parents and former senators Manny and Cynthia Villar, and businessman Paolo Villar.

Mark’s divergence from the bloc came as other minority members face their own legal or political troubles. Apart from the four absentee senators, Padilla was issued a subpoena in relation to the obstruction of justice complaint filed against him over his alleged involvement in Dela Rosa’s escape from Senate premises in May.

Litigator and Free Legal Assistance Group member Raffy Aquino said in a Rappler interview that the Villar siblings’ votes could point to one of two things: they either “demonstrated how it is to vote according to one’s conscience,” or it was a strategy to have a foot on either side of the door. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage
articles.summary: The tenant of the flat in Madrid, Maricarmen, was unable to pay the rent set by the firm which recently bought it.

blocks.text: The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman from the home in Madrid where she lived for seven decades has drawn attention to the depth of Spain's housing crisis.
The tenant of the flat in the Retiro area of central Madrid, Maricarmen, was unable to pay the rent set by the investment firm that owns it.
Maricarmen's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.
However, the company that bought the property in 2018, Urbagestión, cited a legal glitch allowing it to raise her rent from €500 (£428; $572) to €2,650.
It subsequently lowered the new rent to €1,650 but Maricarmen was still unable to pay it with her monthly pension of €1,350.
Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention.

Supporters of Maricarmen camped outside the building on Tuesday night, joined by celebrities including Javier Bardem's brother, Carlos, and the singer Ana Belén, who read out the poem Desahucio (Eviction) by Rafael Alberti.

Several hundred people, mostly youngsters, had gathered by the morning in a bid to prevent the eviction from taking place, chanting "Maricarmen stays". Some activists blocked the stairs inside the building.
In a video posted on social media, a tearful Maricarmen thanked those who had come out to support her against "this cruel struggle by someone who wants to earn money".

The possibility of a last-minute reprieve for Maricarmen appeared when an anonymous donor offered to pay most of her rent. However, Urbagestión reportedly rejected the offer and the eviction went ahead.

"Today is a very sad day, a very dramatic day, when it's plain to see the effects of unbridled speculation, of not wanting to control the market, of putting out the red carpet for the vultures and the speculators," said Housing Minister Teresa Rodríguez.
A shortage of available housing has been blamed for soaring rental costs in recent years, which have left millions of Spaniards struggling to find affordable homes.
In Madrid, rentals have increased by more than 100% over the last decade, according to property site Idealista, with a 10% rise over the last year.

The Socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez has frequently targeted companies whose investment pushes up housing costs. In January, the prime minister said he aimed to "protect those who are most exposed to that speculation and that greed".
However, some critics of the government say it needs to work harder to build new homes, and others warn that its rhetoric discourages many owners from placing their properties on the rental market.

articles.title: Dolly Parton's manager accuses her nephew of threats and intimidation
articles.summary: Bryan Seaver, who announced Parton's death to the world, is accused of trying to extort her estate.

blocks.text: Dolly Parton's management company has accused her nephew of "threats, intimidation, and coercion", revealing a bitter battle over the late star's legacy and business interests.
The accusations against Bryan Seaver, who was Parton's head of security and was handpicked to announce her death last month, have been made public in legal documents filed this week.
The company that manages Parton's businesses and properties, She's Alive, is seeking a temporary civil restraining order against him.

In court filings, She's Alive alleged that Seaver mounted "an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats", claiming he would ruin her empire if the estate did not pay him. He has denied the claims.
In a statement to TMZ, external, he said that text messages and emails quoted in the case had been taken out of context to make it look like he was threatening people.
"Nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by," he said.
"A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving."
Seaver, the son of Parton's sister Cassie, owns a company that provided the singer's security detail for the last 20 years of her life.
Last week, he was fired by She's Alive as head of security for her properties.
In a statement at the time, Seaver and his company said the dismissal was "unexpected" and "unexplained".
They added: "We refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much."
The request for a restraining order was filed in Nashville on Tuesday by She's Alive, which is run by Parton's longtime manager Danny Nozell.
The court documents quoted a series of exchanges in which someone, identified by the estate as Seaver, threatened to destroy Parton's brand.
In one, he said he would become "the hand of retribution for my entire family", according to the court documents.
Another said: "I'm going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It's going to be great. Or [expletive] pay me."
The papers also claimed that Seaver used his experience as a military contractor to intimidate employees.
In an exchange with one of Parton's lawyers, he allegedly described himself as a "killer" and said that on the day his aunt died, he had sold $27m (£20m) in arms and ammunition to the Haitian police.
"All I do is warfare... Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do," he was accused of saying, according to a copy of an email attached to the complaint.
In his statement to TMZ, Seaver said: "I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer."
But he denied making threats and said he had been "talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend".
The messages have resulted in some employees and lawyers for Parton's trusts and estates resigning, according to the court documents.
She's Alive has also had to hire private security for its employees, including at their homes, the filing states.
The BBC has contacted Seaver and She's Alive for further comment.
Previously, Seaver was known to the public for announcing his aunt's death in a video posted to her Instagram account on 25 August.
Speaking in front of a black background, he was sombre and reflective as he introduced himself and shared the unexpected news.
"This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality," he said in the video.
Seaver added that he had followed in his father Larry's footsteps in becoming Parton's head of security, a post he held for more than 20 years.
Nozell started working for Parton in 2004, first as a tour consultant and later as her manager.

In the 2019 Netflix film, Dolly Parton: Here I Am, he said his job was to transform her from a "heritage act" into a "superstar", and he took responsibility for reviving her international touring career.
In a statement last month, he said the singer had "worked up until the day she died" on multiple projects, and envisioned a legacy that continued long beyond her death.
"She loved seeing her dreams come to life, and loved knowing her work brought people joy," he said in the statement.
"Ever the planner, Dolly worked with the team that she handpicked, for the past several years to build a project roadmap that will guide us for decades to come."
The estate now faces a public tug of war over that legacy.

articles.title: PH leads ASEAN, partner navies in West Philippine Sea drills
articles.summary: A Chinese Navy vessel is seen close to where eight countries are sailing for the drills, but it does not respond to challenges from the Philippine Navy

blocks.text: ADMM-PLUS DRILLS. Ten navy vessels from eight different countries sail behind the BRP Jose Rizal on September 23, 2026, during a joint cooperative activity in waters off the coast of Zambales.
Bea Cupin/Rappler
A Chinese Navy vessel is seen close to where eight countries are sailing for the drills, but it does not respond to challenges from the Philippine Navy

items: The Philippines hosted a joint maritime security exercise involving eleven ships from eight countries as part of the ASEAN Defense Ministers' Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) EWG-MS.

The exercises focused on interoperability among regional navies and included drills for medical evacuation, search and rescue, and aiding grounded vessels, while China did not participate in the sea phase despite being present at the opening.

Maritime security in the South China Sea remains a critical concern for ASEAN nations, with ongoing tensions between the Philippines and China over territorial claims, particularly in the West Philippine Sea.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

ABOARD THE BRP JOSE RIZAL – In waters off the coast of Zambales on the morning of Wednesday, September 23, the domineering figure of the helicopter destroyer JS Ise inched closer and closer to the Navy’s flagship, the BRP Jose Rizal.
It was a welcome sight — a signal that a joint activity under the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) would soon commence.

Dotting the waters around Rizal was an impressive array of gray ships — the Philippine Navy’s own BRP Tarlac, two from India, two from New Zealand, and one each from Singapore, Brunei, Australia, the United States, and Japan. All eleven ships from eight countries were in these waters for the sea phase of the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) Experts’ Working Group on Maritime Security (EWG-MS).

ADMM-Plus is the premier platform for the region’s defense ministers to take up a long list of issues. For the ADMM-Plus EWG-MS, the focus was on maritime security and environmental resilience in the face of climate change.

On Wednesday, the Rizal was the lead ship for formation drills and a medical evacuation, while the Japanese forces led search and rescue efforts. The BRP Tarlac, meanwhile, practiced aiding a grounded oil tanker and cross-deck landing drills.

China did not participate in the sea phase of the ADMM-Plus EWG-MS, although they could have. Representatives from China were present at the opening of the ADMM-Plus EWG-MS in Zambales on Monday, September 21.

Reporters embarked on the Rizal, including a team from Rappler, saw at least one People’s Liberation Army Navy or Chinese military warship close to the area where the vessels were sailing together. The Rizal issued radio challenges to the Chinese vessel but did not get a response.
The sea phase and even the meetings on land aren’t just for showing off new and old assets.

They’re meant to test and practice interoperability, or the ability of different navies and units to work with each other. On a more human level, it’s about establishing familiarity and trust between the armed forces of the bloc and its partners.
Aside from chairing ASEAN, Manila is also chair of the ADMM. The Philippines, with Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. as host, is expected to host ministers of the ADMM-Plus before 2026 ends.

“Our collaboration and cooperation not merely in response but in early prepositioning, working together, and in detection becomes more critical,” said Teodoro on Monday, at the opening of the ADMM-Plus EGW-MS.

Alongside the joint cooperative activity is a Future Leaders Program or FLP, which brings junior officers of different navies together to “engage their counterparts on climate change, maritime security, and key topics, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and Critical Underwater Infrastructure security.”

In the region — and in ASEAN especially — maritime security is a major concern. The South China Sea, where up to a third of global trade passes through, encompasses several ASEAN countries. It is also the flashpoint for regional tensions, mostly between Southeast Asian claimant nations and superpower China, which is part of the ADMM-Plus and is an ASEAN dialogue partner.
Malaysia, Vietnam, Brunei, and the Philippines are all claimants to various areas and features of the South China Sea.

Wednesday’s drills were within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone, an area where Manila should have sovereign rights or the exclusive rights to exploit and responsibility to protect marine resources. Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, including the Philippine EEZ, which is part of the West Philippine Sea.
China has also refused to recognize the landmark 2016 Arbitral Award.

Tensions between Manila and Beijing have meant confrontations in the West Philippine Sea for the Philippines’ maritime frontliners. China has had tense confrontations, including skirmishes, with other ASEAN claimants in the past.

ASEAN, with Manila as chair, has aspirations of concluding a Code of Conduct on the South China Sea with China before 2026 ends. Teodoro has publicly cast doubt over Beijing’s trustworthiness. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Ancient wall found beneath Paris could confirm site of first settlement
articles.summary:
Discovery of Gallo-Roman period structure hailed as ‘major breakthrough’ by French culture ministry

An ancient wall discovered beneath Paris has been described as a “major breakthrough” by…

blocks.text: An ancient wall discovered beneath Paris has been described as a “major breakthrough” by France’s culture ministry, with the archaeological find possibly confirming the location of the city’s original settlement.

A roughly 20-metre (65ft) stretch of wall dating from the Gallo-Roman period was discovered in Paris this summer beneath a building on the Île de la Cité, near Notre Dame Cathedral in the heart of the French capital.
The stone-and-wood structure is thought to be a fragment of the ramparts of Lutetia – the ancient name for Paris – built by the Gallic Parisii tribe who lived along the River Seine in the iron age.
The Île de la Cité has traditionally been regarded as the centre of Lutetia, but a rival theory, backed by some archaeological research, contends that it was in Nanterre, a suburb to the west.

blocks.caption: The Gallo-Roman period wall. Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “We may be looking at one of the most important remains ever discovered for understanding Gallic Lutetia,” the culture minister, Catherine Pégard, said in a statement on Wednesday. “Scientific caution still requires that we verify its function and its chronology, but the convergence of evidence is particularly remarkable at this stage.”

Lutetia was first mentioned in book seven of Julius Caesar’s Gallic Wars series, where it was said to be on an island in the River Seine – a vague description that has given rise to many theories about its location.

The wall, uncovered in the course of excavations beneath the Hôtel-Dieu hospital, bears traces of fire, which may correspond to Caesar’s account that the Gauls set fire to their town before the Battle of Lutetia against the Romans.
Carbon dating of the charred evidence dated the find to between 200BC and 10BC, the ministry said in its statement – a timeframe that covers the Battle of Lutetia, in 52BC.
The Île de la Cité is the largest island in the Seine in the Paris region and became the centre of the Roman settlement of Lutetia.

blocks.text: Rebels from the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) have reportedly taken control of regional airports in Tigray, in northern Ethiopia, and further clashed with government forces in the neighboring Afar and Amhara regions.
Wednesday's clashes are the latest of several in recent months and have sparked fears of renewed intense fighting in the war-ravaged region.

The African Union (AU) estimates that some 600,000 people were killed in fighting between the TPLF and Ethiopian forces during a 2020-2022 civil war and that more than 1 million people remain displaced.
On Wednesday, state-owned Ethiopian Airlines announced that it had canceled service at Mekelle, Tigray's capital, as well as Axum and Shire regional airports "due to the current situation."
Local witnesses reported that TPLF rebels armed with light weapons had taken Mekelle Airport — which is normally controlled by government forces — without a fight.

Renewed fighting comes just days after the TPLF announced that it had entered an "Alliance for Survival" with other groups aimed at removing Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and his government from power.
Abiy and his Prosperity Party won reelection in June, though the vote was boycotted by Ethiopia's main opposition groups.
The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 until 2018, when it was replaced by Abiy, whose election sparked the country's civil war.

The Pretoria Peace Agreement brought an end to the conflict, but peace has remained elusive, with government troops resuming drone strikes in 2025 as TPLF rebels began amassing troops at regional borders.
Ethiopia has accused the TPLF of allying with neighboring Eritrea and other armed groups.

An advisor to Prime Minister Abiy called Wednesday's development "heartbreaking," saying rebels had launched offensives against government forces in Afar and Amhara as well as taking control of airports in Tigray.

However, the Tigray army "has been instructed to counter the attack and genocidal invasion launched against us, and has entered into a defensive battle," the Tigray government said in a statement on Facebook.
Ethiopia's broken Tigray peace deal opens old wounds

articles.title: OpenAI gives cyber defence tools to Ukraine
articles.summary: Ukraine will get access to OpenAI's advanced GPT 5.6 Sol model under the deal - a rival to Anthropic's Mythos and Fable

blocks.text: The tech giant OpenAI will share its AI cyber defence system Daybreak for free with the Ukraine government to help it protect civilian infrastructure, like hospitals and power plants, from cyber-attacks.
According to the Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA), the national cyber incident response team, Ukraine recorded nearly 6,000 attacks in 2025.
Daybreak is able to quickly identify weaknesses in digital systems and help develop fixes.
Under the deal, Ukraine will get access to OpenAI's advanced GPT 5.6 Sol model - a rival to Anthropic's Mythos and Fable.

George Osborne, former UK chancellor and now Head of OpenAI for Countries, said: "Protecting civilian infrastructure means defending it against both physical and digital attacks, so people can continue to live, work and access essential services."

Reacting to the news, Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence for the cybersecurity firm Sophos, said that Russian offensive cyber operations had been "a key component" of the Kremlin's aggression against Ukraine since 2014.
"Any initiative that strengthens Ukraine's already highly capable, but heavily burdened, cyber defence efforts is a welcome development and could provide a valuable force multiplier," he said.

Jamie MacColl, a senior research fellow specialising in cyber at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told the BBC western tech firms had been supporting Ukraine for some time - partly for altruistic reasons but also because they gain very valuable data and intelligence from an active conflict.
"Given this, it's no surprise that OpenAI is now also providing defensive cyber security services" he said.
He thought access to Daybreak would be useful, particularly given the volume of Russian cyber-attacks targeting the country.
But he noted Ukraine already had access to AI tools provided by OpenAI's competitors, like Google.
The cyber-abilities of the latest, most powerful AI models, called "frontier" models in AI jargon, can be a boon for cyber-defenders, but the same abilities can also be used for attack.
Spotting weaknesses in systems, for example, is useful for defenders looking to block hackers, but also for attackers hunting for ways to infiltrate an organisation.

Anthropic has tightly restricted access to its systems on the grounds that they are too powerful to fall into the wrong hands, but OpenAI has allowed some firms in Europe, as well as UK banks, to use its most advanced cyber models.
The firm made the announcement alongside the UN General Assembly which is currently underway in New York.
AI is firmly on the agenda there, and US tech bosses including OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei are due to speak at the high-level gathering.
United Nations Secretary General António Guterres called for the tech to be regulated in his final address, while US President Donald Trump says it should be renamed "super intelligence".
Evidence suggests the technology is increasingly being used in the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

In a report published earlier this month, Anthropic claimed that its Claude platform appeared to have been used by a group of Russian developers to build software for a swarm of so-called "kamikaze" drones designed for attacks in Ukraine.
It said the group had activated virtual private networks - VPNs - in order to get around a geographical block put in place by the tech firm.
Anthropic also claimed AI had been used in attempts to infiltrate the Ukrainian government, military and diplomatic services.

Recently, around 100 US companies signed an open letter warning governments and institutions around the world that "the window is closing" to ensure cyber defences are robust enough to withstand AI-enabled cyber attacks.

But it's not just bad actors deploying the tech that are of growing concern: in the summer, OpenAI revealed that a group of AI agents it had been testing had escaped from their controls, and secretly worked together to hack to another tech firm, Hugging Face.
Anthropic, and Google subsequently revealed similar incidents.
Additional reporting by Chris Vallance

articles.title: Police use teargas on protesters as disabled woman, 87, evicted from Madrid home
articles.summary:
Housing rights campaigners decry landlord’s ‘barbaric behaviour’ after apartment Maricarmen had lived in for 71 years was bought by a developer

There were violent scenes in Madrid on…

blocks.text: There were violent scenes in Madrid on Wednesday as riot police fought with protesters trying to prevent the eviction of a disabled 87-year-old woman from her apartment in the El Retiro district of the city.

Hundreds of protesters had gathered, many of them overnight, in an effort to block the fourth attempt to carry out the eviction. Activists from the Madrid and Barcelona tenants’ union, and celebrities including the actor Carlos Bardem and the singer and actor Ana Belén, also joined the protest.

Police fired rounds of teargas and repeatedly baton-charged the protesters as they tried to open a path for the judicial committee to carry out the eviction order, which was eventually executed on Wednesday morning.
The tenant, known simply by her first name Maricarmen, has 50% disability and is about to turn 88.

blocks.caption: Maricarmen is overwhelmed by emotion at an event organised by housing activists the day before her eviction. Photograph: David Canales/SOPA Images/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Demonstrators chanted “Ayuso’s attic for Maricarmen”, a reference to the scandal surrounding the Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso’s alleged purchase with public money of a €6.3m residential apartment for her use as a temporary office.
Behind the locked door, more protesters occupied the staircase leading to Maricarmen’s flat while neighbours handed out snacks and offered the demonstrators the use of their bathroom.
When a developer bought the building Maricarmen had lived in for 71 years, she was offered the chance to buy her apartment for €247,000 (£212,000), an impossible sum for a pensioner.

They then raised her rent from €500 to €1,650 a month, while she receives a state pension of €1,350. An unnamed “prominent” writer offered to pay the €1,150 difference indefinitely but their offer was ignored.

In a video recorded this morning by the local tenants’ union, a tearful Maricarmen said: “Good morning, everyone, I thank you for the action you are taking, spending the whole night sleeping in the street. Please, keep going, but don’t hurt one another. This has to be peaceful.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators rally against Maricarmen’s eviction in Madrid’s El Retiro neighbourhood. Photograph: David Canales/SOPA Images/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “I can still hear all your noise. A hug to everyone and to all the people who are supporting me in this cruel struggle against a person who wants to make money but who should not forget that they have parents and that one day they could find themselves in the situation that, unfortunately, I am in.”

The original 1956 contract for the flat was in Maricarmen’s father’s name; when he died, the apartment passed to his wife, and on her death in 2008 was then sublet to Maricarmen. The landlords, Urbagestión SL, successfully argued in the supreme court that this subletting was invalid and that the contract was no longer valid. Urbagestión SL has been approached for comment.

Speaking at the scene, Aldo Reverte, spokesperson for the Confederation of Tenants’ Unions, said: “Maricarmen’s case is just one more example of what happens when housing is put in the hands of landlords. The difference is that a lot of people have become aware of her situation and the tenants’ union has shown that we can fight this type of barbaric behaviour.”

However, for all their efforts, the protesters were unable to stop the eviction. Beatriz Duro, the lawyer representing Maricarmen, said: “The owner isn’t prepared to negotiate or accept any sort of offer. We have asked for a place where we can take Maricarmen’s personal belongings.”
So far this year, 4,000 evictions have been carried out in Spain.
