articles.title: Jonvic Remulla admits error on Harry Roque’s asylum status
articles.summary: In an interview with reporters on Tuesday, September 22, Remulla said that Roque's status is currently "in limbo.”

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 4:44pm
In a video uploaded on Nov. 25, 2025, Harry Roque says he will file a motion for reconsideration after a court approved the Philippine government’s request to cancel his passport.
Harry Roque via Facebook / Philstar.com's screenshot
MANILA, Philippines — Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla admitted he was mistaken regarding his previous claims that former presidential spokesperson Harry Roque’s asylum application had been denied.
In an interview with reporters on Tuesday, September 22, Remulla said that Roque's status is currently "in limbo.”
“I was wrong...status now is in limbo,” Remulla said.
According to Remulla, while a decision on an asylum application is normally handed down within six months, Roque's case remains unresolved despite nine months having passed since he applied.
“In his case, it's neither denied nor accepted. So under the eyes of the law, he still does not have asylum,” Remulla said.
(In his case, it is neither denied nor accepted. So in the eyes of the law, he still does not have asylum.)
Remulla also said they are assessing whether an individual granted asylum would be immune from an Interpol red notice.
“We think that there is no reason not to bring him in,” he said.
On September 15, Remulla claimed that Roque’s asylum bid had been denied, which was disputed by the former human rights lawyer.
Roque is currently facing non-bailable qualified human trafficking charges tied to the raided Lucky South 99 POGO hub in Porac, Pampanga, and remains in Austria, where he is seeking asylum.
An Angeles City court ordered his arrest in May 2025, following his undocumented departure from the Philippines in 2024 as law enforcement began hunting for him.

articles.title: DOLE sets guidelines for workers’ protection from air hazards
articles.summary: The guidelines in assessing workers’ exposure to “elevated air pollutants” were outlined in Labor Advisory No. 15 released on Monday, September 21.

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 4:40pm

This aerial photo taken from a commercial plane shows haze from Indonesian forest fires blanketing a residential district in Kuching, the capital city of Sarawak state on the island of Borneo on September 5, 2026.
AFP / Mohd Rasfan
MANILA, Philippines — Private sector employers are directed to implement safety protocols to protect workers from air hazards under the Department of Labor and Employment’s (DOLE) new labor advisory.
The guidelines in assessing workers’ exposure to “elevated air pollutants” were outlined in Labor Advisory No. 15 released on Monday, September 21.

Under the directive, employers are required to conduct a Hazard Identification, Risk Assessment, and Control (HIRAC) to determine their workers’ exposure to smoke, haze and other air pollutants and to prevent potential health dangers.

The Air Quality Index Matrix and Action Points (AQIMAP) issued by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) and the Department of Health (DOH) was recommended to be used as the basis in conducting the assessment.

“The HIRAC shall be reviewed and updated periodically and whenever there is a material change in the AQIMAP level, workplace conditions, nature or extent of workers' exposure, or other circumstances that may affect the assessed risk,” DOLE’s advisory reads.
The labor agency’s advisory came after reports of poor and unhealthy air quality in Metro Manila earlier this month, as smoke and haze from forest fires in Indonesia reached the Philippines.
Implementation
The labor agency also laid out the specific ideal responses of employers for each air quality index (AQI) level.

For unhealthy levels, employers are advised to monitor the air quality levels, provide personal protective equipment in case outdoor work is unavoidable, improve ventilation in enclosed areas, and limit or reschedule outdoor activities.
“Personal protective equipment shall not be used as a substitute for feasible engineering or administrative controls,” the advisory read.

Meanwhile, for acutely unhealthy air quality, employers are urged to implement flexible work arrangements. Workers who are required to report to work physically must be provided with appropriate protective equipment.
In times of emergency, employers are advised to suspend work.
Those who are involved in public utilities and health services are encouraged to maintain a skeleton force, or minimum personnel, to continue operations.

articles.title: Famine threatens the Ukrainian town of Oleshky in the southern Kherson region as Russia delays creating a humanitarian evacuation corridor
articles.summary: Food supplies to the town of Oleshky in the occupied part of the southern Kherson region have been cut off since May. Efforts by Kyiv to negotiate the evacuation of civilians with Moscow have been…

image.caption: The town of Oleshky has been cut off from food deliveries since May, prompting famine for the around 6,000 residents left in the townImage: VALENTYN OGIRENKO/REUTERS

blocks.text: A man sends a photo of "Oleshky borsch," a vegetable soup he has made from leftovers. To make the soup more filling, he says he has added millet and two eggs.

"Today, we have a delicacy in our borsch. My mother traded 2.5 kilograms (5.5 pounds) of sugar for 10 eggs," he tells the recipient of the photo, Tetiana Hasanenko, the head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, which is based in territory controlled by Kyiv. "There's no cabbage in it, but there is asparagus," he adds.

Hasanenko says she's used to getting such messages. "I receive reports like this every day," Hasanenko told DW. "People want to be given some kind of hope, but there is no hope." She said food was last delivered to the town at the end of May. "The situation is critical," she said, warning that "you can't just call this starvation — it's a famine."

Oleshky is located in Ukraine'ssouthern Kherson region on the left bank of the Dnipro River. The city has been occupied since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion.Russia's full-scale invasionin February 2022.
In June 2023, the town was almost completely flooded after a blast at the Kakhovka Power Plant and the breach of the Kakhovka Dam.

Hasanenko said the situation worsened last winter. She said there were about 6,000 people left in the area, including 180 children. They have already become accustomed to living without electricity and gas and have to fetch water from wells. Now, they have to prepare for another harsh winter.

blocks.caption: The destruction of the Kakhovka Dam in southern Ukraine has flooded Oleshky and left many basements full of food inaccessible for monthsImage: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: 'One kilo of zucchini for 1,000 rubles'

"To be honest, I haven't eaten anything yet," resident Halyna (whose name has been changed for security reasons) told DW by phone at around lunchtime. "My best option for today is a flatbread made of water and flour, as there's still some left. I spread apple sauce on it and make myself some tea without sugar. That's about it."

People only go out between 7 a.m. and 9 a.m., she explained, adding that they tended to gather in the market square to hear the latest news and would trade or sell food from their supplies or gardens.

"Today, there were a few zucchinis for 1,000 rubles (€10 or $11.4) per kilo," she said, adding that someone had sold a large sack of flour for 200,000 rubles. She speculated that he was probably going to try to leave Oleshky, which is why the price was so high.

Minibuses used to run from Oleshky to Skadovsk about an hour south and then to Crimea or Russia. They also transported food to Oleshky for sale. After they were attacked by drones, two ambulances were deployed instead. "But for the past month and a half, none of the ambulances have been running, because one of the drivers was killed on a trip," Halyna reported.
She explained that people are now stocking up on food in the village of Radensk, located 20 kilometers (12.4 miles) to the south. People walk there or ride their bikes.

Anyone who wants to be evacuated must reach the village of Tarasivka, which is another 20 kilometers away. From there, you can get to Skadovsk by minibus or by hitchhiking. However, the route is heavily mined. "You set out and could die along the way," Halyna said, adding that two women who were trying to get food died that way.
According to Halyna, scores of people in Oleshky have been injured by mines and explosive devices. But they can't count on medical help.

"If your leg is blown off, you're as good as dead. There's a surgeon at the hospital, but no anesthesiologist and no medicine," she said. Conditions are also deteriorating for inpatients. "Last winter, they still got some soup and two pieces of baked dough," she said, adding that now there's one and a half spoonfuls of semolina porridge cooked in water and cold tea.
Moreover, evacuating from Oleshky is difficult not only because of the danger of landmines. Many residents have neither a Russian nor a Ukrainian passport. In addition, people lack cash.

blocks.caption: Ukrainian authorities say that Russia has been slow in creating a humanitarian evacuation corridor for the trapped civiliansImage: Metin Aktas/Anadolu Agency/picture alliance

blocks.text: Moscow lacks evacuation willingness

"There is only one solution: A 'green corridor' must be established and the people evacuated. The occupying authorities must move the people deeper into the temporarily occupied territory," says Tetiana Hasanenko of the Ukrainian military administration.

Talks about an evacuation from Oleshky have been ongoing since last spring. At that time, at the initiative of the Ukrainian parliamentary human rights commissioner, Dmytro Lubinets, city officials compiled a list of residents who wish to leave the municipality of Oleshky.

"358 people need to be evacuated urgently," he wrote on social media. "These are only the ones we've heard about," he emphasized, noting that the town of Oleshky currently has more than 6,000 residents. "These people must be rescued because the town has become a death trap," the ombudsman said.

According to him, preliminary agreements had been reached between Kyiv and Moscow. The Ukrainian military was to ensure a ceasefire, and the International Committee of the Red Cross was to assist with the evacuation. But Russia "has not reaffirmed its willingness" to carry out the evacuation "for quite some time," Lubinets said.

Meanwhile, the residents of Oleshky are desperate, says Tetiana Hasanenko. "They had hoped that the evacuation would begin at any moment. But what now? I can't give them any hope at all," she laments.
Russia steps up drone attacks on Ukraine's Kherson
This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

articles.title: Malacañang dismisses 'presidential pork barrel' claim on LGSF as intrigue
articles.summary: Malacañang on Wednesday again defended the proposed P58.53-billion allocation for the Local Government Support Fund (LGSF) in the 2027 national budget after critics, led by Caloocan City Rep. Edgar…

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 4:22pm

Malacañang on Wednesday again defended the proposed P58.53-billion allocation for the Local Government Support Fund (LGSF) in the 2027 national budget after critics, led by Caloocan City Rep. Edgar Erice, described it as a “presidential pork barrel.”
Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said describing the LGSF as a presidential pork barrel was merely “pang-intriga” (for intrigue).

“Karapatan niyang tumakbo kahit saang korte pero dapat siguraduhin lamang po niya na mayroong basehan dahil kung mabibigyan lamang siya o aaralin po niya ang proseso kung paano nairi-release ang LGSF sa mga LGU (local government units), malamang ay maliwanagan po siya,” Castro said, referring to Erice.

(It is his right to go to whatever court, but he should make sure that there is a basis because if he is given [the information], or if he studies the process of how the LGSF is released to LGUs, he will likely be enlightened.)

Castro made the statement in response to Erice’s questioning of the proposed LGSF allocation under the 2027 National Expenditure Program and his suggestion that he could bring the matter before the Supreme Court if necessary.

Erice said granting the executive department the power to decide on LGSF allocations effectively gives the President a “blank check” and amounts to Congress abdicating its constitutionally mandated power of the purse.

Erice has repeatedly cited the LGSF allocation granted to Naga City for the rehabilitation of the Jesse Robredo Coliseum. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. personally presented the allocation to Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo, which Erice said gave the impression that the administration was courting her as a potential candidate.
Castro said that although she did not want to mention Robredo’s name again in the issue, the Naga City mayor had already explained how the local government applied for the LGSF.

“As soon as I assumed office in 2025, I tried to look for funding already for its rehabilitation. It was difficult because of the big amount that is required. Senator Kiko Pangilinan advised me that we could apply for LGSF funding because of the nature of the project, which we did,” Robredo wrote in a Facebook post.
Castro also pointed to the Supreme Court’s ruling in Belgica v. Executive Secretary, which she said did not prohibit the LGSF.
“Hindi po ipinagbabawal ng Supreme Court ang LGSF,” Castro said.
(The Supreme Court does not prohibit the LGSF.)

The Supreme Court, in its 2013 ruling in Belgica v. Ochoa, declared the Priority Development Assistance Fund (PDAF) and similar congressional pork barrel mechanisms unconstitutional, saying they allowed lawmakers to intervene in the post-enactment stages of budget execution.
The Court also struck down provisions granting broad discretion to the President over certain lump-sum funds for failing to meet the constitutional requirement of sufficient standards.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Mark Villar, facing graft complaints, breaks from minority on VP Sara threshold vote
articles.summary: Sen. Mark Villar twice strayed from the Senate minority bloc on Wednesday, September 23, by abstaining from his bloc's bid to block the threshold vote, then joining the majority in lowering the bar…

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 4:22pm
Senator-judge Mark Villar attends Day 2 of the impeachment trial at the Senate in Pasay City.
Mark Villar via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Mark Villar twice strayed from the Senate minority bloc on Wednesday, September 23, by abstaining from his bloc's bid to block the threshold vote, then joining the majority in lowering the bar for convicting Vice President Sara Duterte.

Villar was the only minority senator to take part in the second vote that sought to settle the question raised by Sen. Erwin Tulfo whether the 16-bar threshold for conviction should still hold given four senators' absence from the trial.
Thirteen senators including Villar voted in favor, while Presiding Officer Sen. Chiz Escudero cast the lone vote against overturning the ruling he himself issued when the trial opened in July.

The rest of the minority bloc members chose to boycott the proceedings and keep out of the chamber during the vote, namely Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano, Sen. Pia Cayetano, Sen. Bong Go, Sen. Imee Marcos, Sen. Camille Villar and Sen. Robin Padilla.

Cayetano earlier raised a point of order in an attempt to prevent the court from holding a vote at all. He argued the court had no authority to reopen the threshold in the middle of the trial and that the question belonged to the Supreme Court.

To address Cayetano's point of order, Escudero divided the house and called for a vote. Thirteen senator-judges voted to shoot down Cayetano's appeal, while the five other minority senators present backed Cayetano. Villar abstained.
Legal issues

Both Mark and Camille Villar are among the members of their family facing criminal and administrative complaints the Ombudsman filed last Friday over PrimeWater Infrastructure Corp.'s water district deals.

The agency found the joint ventures grossly disadvantageous to the government. It identified the senator, who served as public works secretary from 2016 to 2021 under then-President Rodrigo Duterte, as the company's beneficial owner.

It was against this backdrop that Camille made a rare emotional interjection earlier Wednesday to urge her colleagues to stop invoking the criminal cases of the senators who have missed the trial. Two of the four, Senators Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada, are detained on nonbailable plunder charges.

"Lahat naman po ng wala dito, hindi naman po sila napatunayan na may sala. Hindi po sila plunderer. Hindi po sila magnanakaw," she said. (Those who are not here have not been proven guilty. They are not plunderers. They are not thieves).

She was answering Sen. Erwin Tulfo, who had argued that the framers of the 1987 Constituion never anticipated senators facing plunder charges, since those in their time faced subversion, sedition and rebellion.
Tulfo later said he had called no one a convicted plunderer and was merely speaking of the reality that four senators cannot take part in the trial.
Hours later, Camille left the chamber with the rest of the bloc. After the lunch break, she was seen briefly returning to the Chamber and conversing with her brother before leaving.
The court ruled on Wednesday that the two-thirds needed to convict will be computed only from senators legally and factually capable of taking part when the verdict is called.
Excluded are senators who are detained, suspended, medically incapacitated or beyond the Senate's coercive processes and others similarly situated.

articles.title: Minority member Mark Villar votes for lower threshold
articles.summary: Senator Mark Villar on Wednesday voted "yes" to lower the threshold to convict Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial, despite being a member of the senate minority.

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 4:04pm
Senator Mark Villar on Wednesday voted "yes" to lower the threshold to convict Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial, despite being a member of the senate minority.
He was the lone senator from the minority to do so as Senate minority leader Alan Peter Cayetano, and five others from the group did not participate in the voting.
Among them, Senators Pia Cayetano, Christopher "Bong" Go, Imee Marcos, Robin Padilla, and Mark's sister, Camille Villar.
Senator Mark Villar has yet to give an explanation on his vote. His sister, Camille, has also yet to issue a statement.
GMA News Online has reached out to Mark Villar for comment, but he has yet to reply as of posting time.

The Senate impeachment court on Wednesday has voted to lower the threshold required to convict Duterte in her impeachment trial by setting it to two-thirds of the senator-judges who are legally allowed to participate in the proceedings.

Thirteen senator-judges voted in favor of the motion put forward by Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo, who sought reconsideration of the July 6 ruling that set the voting threshold at 16 which is two-thirds of the 24-member Senate.

“It means that for purposes of determining the two-thirds concurrence vote required for conviction under Article 11, Section 3.6, the phrase 'All members of the Senate' shall refer only to those members who, at the time of the vote, remain legally and factually capable of participating in the impeachment proceedings," Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero said.
He said excluded members are those:

items: detained and/or suspended or otherwise legally restrained from exercising the functions of a senator,
persons sought by authorities and whose whereabouts are unknown,
suffering from a physical or medical incapacity,
beyond the coercive processes of the Senate, and
others similarly situated.

blocks.text: “The remaining [qualified] members shall then constitute the denominator from which the required two- thirds concurrence shall be computed. When the computation of two-thirds results in a fraction, the number of votes required for conviction shall be rounded up to the next higher whole number, even if the fraction is less than 0.5,” Escudero added.
Tulfo sought consideration since four of their colleagues have not been present in the impeachment trial proceedings.

Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained on plunder and other related charges due to their alleged involvement in flood control projects and undeclared campaign donations, respectively.

Senator Ronald dela Rosa, on the other hand, is nowhere to be found amid a standing warrant of arrest issued against him by the International Criminal Court due to his alleged involvement in the drug war deaths.
Senator Loren Legarda, for her part, is on an extended medical leave abroad due to a lung ailment.
The 1987 Constitution states that "no person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate." —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: In the Public Square: Making sense of the BARMM elections

The country passed through a historic moment only a few days ago — but how many Filipinos were even aware of it? The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao held its first parliamentary elections, with 80 seats in the regional parliament and the future of peace and development at stake.

articles.title: Sara Duterte now participating in impeachment trial 'with caution'
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte is now participating in her impeachment trial with caution after the Senate voted to lower the voting threshold for her conviction, her defense team said Wednesday.

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 4:02pm
Vice President Sara Duterte is now participating in her impeachment trial with caution after the Senate voted to lower the voting threshold for her conviction, her defense team said Wednesday.

Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison made the manifestation on Day 29 of Duterte's impeachment trial, shortly after senator-judges voted 13-1-6 to set the conviction threshold at two-thirds of those who are legally allowed to participate in the proceedings.

"Even as we understand that this tribunal will proceed as it deems fit, we nonetheless are constrained to place on record, na mula sa araw na ito, the respondent's participation or any participation that the respondent will have in this trial ay may tahasang pag-iingat or with ad cautelam," said Sison, referring to the Latin phrase which means "with caution."

(Even as we understand that this tribunal will proceed as it deems fit, we nonetheless are constrained to place on record that from this day forward, the respondent's participation or any participation that the respondent will have in this trial will carry outright caution or with ad cautelam.)
Sison stressed that the vice president is not trying to evade accountability amid the ongoing impeachment trial against her.

"Let it be clear that the respondent does not shrink from accountability nor does she fear the outcome of this impeachment trial. She asks for nothing spectacular from this court. Only the most essential and basic guarantees due to every individual: fairness and impartiality," Sison said.
With the new decision on the voting threshold, Duterte can be convicted with less than 16 votes as several senators are facing charges, remain in hiding, or remain on medical leave.
The interpretation of the phrase "All members of the Senate"—referring to the base number to compute the two-thirds requirement—has been the subject of debate.
Sison said Duterte has the right to pursue all legal remedies in the wake of the ruling.

"She reserves every right to exhaust all legal remedies available sa ilalim ng ating batas at Konstitusyon na may pagtatangi sa esensya ng isang tunay na malayang, demokratikong institusyon. At karapatan ng bawat mamamayan na madinig sa isang hukuman na walang kinikilingan o kinakatakutan," she added.

(She reserves every right to exhaust all legal remedies available under our law and Constitution, with due regard for the essence of a truly free, democratic institution. And it is the right of every citizen to be heard in an impartial court that fears no one.)

Thirteen senators voted in favor of the motion put forward by Senator-Judge Erwin Tulfo, who sought reconsideration of the July 6 ruling that the voting threshold is set at 16, or a fixed two-thirds computation of the complete 24-member Senate.
Six minority senators, on the other hand, did not participate in the voting.

In early September, the impeachment court invited retired Supreme Court Chief Justices Artemio Panganiban, Reynato Puno, and Hilario Davide Jr. and Associate Justice Adolfo Azcuna as amici curiae or friends of the court to share their views on the matter.
Panganiban, Puno, and Davide said that the voting threshold should be based on the number of senator-judges who actively participated in the impeachment trial.

However, Azcuna, one of the framers of the 1987 Constitution, offered a different view that the two-thirds concurrence requirement should relate to the entire membership of the Senate; hence, a conviction by 16 senator-judges is needed. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Robert Pattinson's Primetime hates Chris Hansen
articles.summary: Primetime is a chaotic, spiralling dark comedy is off-putting and strange. But more than that, it attempts to take down Chris Hansen.

image.caption: Robert Pattinson appears as Chris Hansen in a still from A24's Primetime. Director Lance Oppenheim and writer Ajon Singh aim to expose a deep rot at the centre of the NBC crime series To Catch a Predator. (Elevation Pictures)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Primetime is a chaotic, spiralling dark comedy is off-putting and strange. But more than that, it attempts to take down Chris Hansen.
Lance Oppenheim directed takedown of Chris Hansen's To Catch a Predator pulls no punches
It's 9 p.m. on a Wednesday. Do you know where your children are?

If you're the fictionalized version of To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen portrayed by Robert Pattinson in A24's Primetime, you're convinced you do — at least, you've convinced your network you know where everybody else's are.

This Hansen explains, drink in hand, to his airplane seatmate: it's what got his show greenlit in the first place. As he tells his executives, children aren't off roaming the streets or falling down wells. They're alone in their rooms. But outside, Hansen says, is a man standing on the porch, genitalia in hand. And in movie-Hansen's shockingly vulgar description that we're not going to fully quote here: he's about to charge up to that bedroom.
But if his audience just watches To Catch a Predator tonight on NBC, Hansen pitches, he'll tell them how to stop him.

The value of that advice he's offering is obvious to anyone familiar with what happened on that 2004 show. The Dateline series had Hansen pop out of closets and bedrooms to confront alleged child predators his team had lured there — and that infamously led to failed prosecutions, dangerous copycats and at least one death.

But Primetime is anything but a strait-laced critique. What spins out from the movie charting this fraught history is a whirligig of obscenity and oddity. It's a chaotic, spiralling dark comedy. And one so off-putting (it is produced by The Strange Thing About the Johnsons' Ari Aster, after all) you're not even shocked when it pairs that offhand humour with stomach-churning horror.

We see Tony Revolori (Spider-Man: Homecoming) making bug-eyed, intentionally ridiculous faces at the camera along with images of butchered children's bodies abandoned in a nameless jungle. We see Pattinson's Hansen inexplicably projectile-spitting mouthwash into a sink — while standing in a bent-arms, leaned-forward pose that looks less like a journalist, and more like an attacking goose.

And then, later, we see that same goose-man chasing down an actual monster, a personification of what is supposedly lurking outside of society. But as he keeps looking for that evil outside of himself, and stares into the face of evil, we stare right back into his.

There's a high-wire act of unself-conscious commitment-to-the-bit that Pattinson so often brings to his roles: a seeming incapability to feel embarrassment that allows him to dive completely into accents, impersonations and general absurdity.

Here, that's a campy, elevated, Spirit Halloween version of Chris Hansen: one that drawls "Why don't you take a seat" with a gravelly self-seriousness that, in anyone else's hands, would just read as ridiculous.

As director Lance Oppenheim and writer Ajon Singh would have us believe, all those over-the-top affectations are really meant to expose a deep rot at the centre of the real man. Because based as it is on the blistering article "Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die," about a shocking outcome to one of his stings, Primetime is not exactly a fan of Hansen's Dateline series. Echoing criticism — and even court rulings — against the ensuing "Creep Catcher" groups that would copy To Catch a Predator's modus operandi, this screenplay offers deep and obvious condemnations.
Which makes it evident as to why the real Chris Hansen hasn't exactly made himself a friend to the project.

Instead, he says he bought his own trailers ahead of the movie, to say the story you're about to see is completely fabricated. Like the Church of Latter-day Saints did in the Playbill for The Book of Mormon, he'll point audiences toward his own tome of content where, he says, the true story lies.

The true-crime streaming network he's since built continues to release content around sexual offences. An unending slew of new shows follow the format of, and capitalize on audiences' insatiable appetite for, the public-shaming vigilantism of To Catch a Predator.

items: Documentary on aftermath of Windsor, Ont.'s Creeper Hunter to premiere at Toronto's Hot Docs Festival
6 teens charged after string of assaults linked to 'Catch a Predator' trend, police say

blocks.text: The critical read of Primetime's funhouse-mirror interpretation is right there. Instead of giving Predator's seemingly righteous goals even a tiny bit of credit, Oppenheim makes it his rhetorical aim to deliberately deconstruct Hansen's assumed self-interest while unreservedly humanizing his targets.

Throughout Hansen's interactions with a harried and hapless producer (Merritt Wever), a clearly traumatized and exploited "decoy" actor used for luring these alleged criminals (Skyler Gisondo) and the empathetically depicted subjects themselves, Primetime's message is clear.

Glassy-eyed, preening and frantic Hansen does not run Predator as some sacred calling, the film says. He does not manipulate local police forces into bypassing laws around search and seizure, wake up his barely grade-school sons in the middle of the night to watch his latest catch or stare hatefully at NBC reporter Stone Phillips reporting on "real" news because he's performing some sacred calling.
In the eyes of Primetime, he's doing it because he wants just that: to be on prime time.

That alone wouldn't be enough. The idea that respectability died first on the airwaves is obvious to the point of insulting; it wasn't enough to float the sci-fi commentary on capitalism The Running Man last year, and it's not enough to float the Rupert Murdoch/Larry Lamb biopic Ink that showed at this year's TIFF.

Neither is it enough to merely acknowledge the existential fear around stranger danger that has fuelled political campaigns and platforms of the past 50 years. From the genuinely moving, loosely inspired adaptation of six-year-old Etan Patz's disappearance in Without a Trace to the abysmally exploitative child-trafficking film Sound of Freedom, the blinding fear around the vulnerability of children already clearly motivates us.

What Primetime gets at is more probative, and more unsettling. A question not necessarily about self-delusion, but about how a lack of humanity seems justified, even encouraged, when dealing with Hansen's subjects.
It's a topic raised by that same airplane seatmate, who asks Hansen whether he ever wants to skip the justice system and just "bleed" the men he catches.
And it's a proposition Hansen considers, then says that just maybe, what he's doing is worse. And then he smiles.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: PM’s new anti-disinformation unit won’t target ‘domestic politcal dissent’, defence secretary says – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Wes Streeting told GB News: ‘We’re not interested in policing domestic political dissent’

Good morning. Andy Burnham delivered his speech to the United Nations in what…

blocks.text: Good morning. Andy Burnham delivered his speech to the United Nations in what felt like the middle of the night in UK time and he announced that he is setting up what he is calling a National Centre for Information Defence.

Burnham said this was necessary because “over the last decade we have given too much ground to those who want to run a negative, corrosive narrative about life in Britain, which bears no resemblance to reality”.

Over at GB News they seem a bit worried this morning about the prospect of a crackdown on corrosive narratives about Britain which bear no resemblance to reality, and it is running a story with a headline referencing “free speech fears” and a quote from a rightwing commentator claiming the Burnham speech was all “talk of control and censorship – exactly the kind of messaging that the Trump administration absolutely hates”.

But close reading of the speech makes it clear that Burnham is not aiming his fire at any parts of the UK media. Burnham said he was concerned about hostile state actors waging disinformation warfare, especially Russia. He told the UN:

double quotation markIn recent years we have seen an industrial-scale assault by hostile actors on the information environment in the UK and that of many of our allies. Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people’s fears. They’ve used bots and fake websites. Falsified newspaper articles. Forged the branding of 28 British organisations – including universities and the BBC. They’ve amplified far-right narratives. And we have evidence that they tried to interfere with the 2019 general election.

(Burnham did not address the fact that there are some within the Trump administration who have also been amplifying far-right narratives with claims about the UK which certainly count as misinformation, and arguably meet the disinformation threshold too.)

Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has been giving interviews this morning and, speaking to GB News, he was asked about claims that Burnham’s new unit could be used against Britons who” simply disagree” with the government. That would not happen, he said.
He told the programme:

double quotation markOne of the great things about Britain, and one of the things that I have a responsibility to defend, is the freedom and democracy that we all enjoy. And that includes the freedom to disagree, the freedom for people to challenge their government, to challenge government policy, to criticise robustly what we are doing and then to have the opportunity to choose a different government. That is a stark contrast to the position that our friends the Russian people endure under the political system that they suffer under. Russia is just one of a number of malign state and non-state actors that seek to threaten and disrupt our democracy, including through misinformation and disinformation.
Streeting added:
double quotation markWe’re not interested in policing domestic political dissent.
You can read Burnham’s UN speech in full here. I will be posting more from it soon.

The Commons is still in recess, and most people in government are getting ready for the Labour conference next week, and so there is almost nothing in the Westminster diary. But there was enough news at the UN yesterday to pad out the week, and so I’m sure there will be enough to cover.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: World lagging on key UN biodiversity targets
articles.summary: Hundreds of nations signed on to a goal to protect 30% of the world's land and sea by 2030. As the timeline reaches the halfway point, activists say the current protection estimates are way behind.

image.caption: Only 10% of global oceans are currently designated for conservation and could only reach 12% by 2030, the research revealsImage: DW

blocks.text: World governments are off track to meet a historic United Nations target to protect at least 30% of the planet's land and seas by the year 2030, according to a new study published Wednesday.

The research by environmental groups Campaign for Nature and Together for the Ocean shows that about 20% of land and inland waters are designated as protected or conserved, following the signing of the 30×30 goal in 2022.
If nations fully deliver on existing quantified commitments, the estimate could increase to 27% by the turn of the decade, the report said.

The 30x30 goal was adopted under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework at COP15 and was signed by nearly 200 nations that pledged at least $200 billion (about €175 billion) annually to reduce biodiversity loss.
Only 'a third' of target reached in ocean protection
For the world's oceans, the study says protection is "lagging."
The coverage is currently at 10% of global ocean and could only reach 12% by 2030, the research revealed.

"The ocean is emerging as one of the defining implementation challenges of 30×30," Together for the Ocean said, adding that important marine ecosystems, like offshore and deep-sea habitats, remain "vulnerable."
Last month, the Convention on Biological Diversity, the UN treaty dedicated to the global nature goals, also cautioned that countries were not on track.
Funding gap
The report singled out finance for conservation as "one of the greatest barriers" to reaching global targets.
The research said that between $100 billion and $180 billion was needed each year to make the 2030 target. Current annual spending, however, amounted to just $24 billion.
"The gap is particularly stark for the ocean, where approximately $16 billion is needed annually, but only an estimated $ 1.8 billion is currently spent," the study said.
From October 19, the UN biodiversity summit in Yerevan will see the nations address the progress shortfall and assess ways of getting back on target.

blocks.text: Here is a roundup of headline stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, September 23, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click hereClick here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
September 23, 2026
ADAC calls to drop once-a-day price rise rule for fuel

The ADAC motoring association has said that a rule in force since April 1 allowing gas stations to raise fuel prices only once a day, at noon, has not brought down prices and "should therefore be abolished."
Although the rule had greatly reduced the number of price changes throughout a day and made increases easier to predict, the gap between the highest and lowest prices had increased, the ADAC said.
It also said motorists who needed to buy gas shortly after noon, when gas stations have typically jacked up prices, were faced with unjustifiably higher costs.
An economic research institute, ZEW, also found in April that prices were higher on average after the rule was introduced, with fuel prices generally going up after noon and cheaper in the morning.
Fuel prices in Germany and Europe in general have skyrocketed amid the war in the Middle East.

The ADAC reported that average gas prices in Germany hit a record high on Thursday, reaching €2.308 for a liter of super E10 and €2.471 for a liter of diesel ($9.98/US gallon and $10.69/US gallon, respectively)

In its statement, the ADAC, however, welcomed the government's temporary reduction in the energy tax that is planned to go into force on October 1, saying it was the most realistic way to lower the burden on motorists.

articles.title: Gus Lamont’s parents make emotional plea as $1m reward offered for information about disappearance
articles.summary:
No trace of Gus has been found since he went missing from his family’s South Australian farm on 27 September last year

The parents of missing four-year-old Gus Lamont have made an emotional…

blocks.text: The parents of missing four-year-old Gus Lamont have made an emotional plea for any information about their “unique little boy” as authorities offered a $1 million reward over the disappearance.
No trace of Gus has been found since he went missing from his family’s enormous sheep farm in the South Australian outback almost a year ago.
Gus’s parents, Joshua Lamont and Jessica Murray pleaded with the public to come forward with any information, no matter how small.
It had been “the most devastating and inexplicable event we have ever experienced”, Murray said in a video message released on Wednesday.
“Our memories of Gus are of a beautiful, sweet, and unique little boy who loved music, listening to stories, and playing in the natural world.
“During the time Gus has been missing, he should have celebrated his fifth birthday and his little brother’s first birthday with us.”
A tearful Lamont said they were desperate for answers.
“We believe that someone knows something. Someone knows what happened to Gus, and may even know where he is,” he said.

South Australian police Det Supt Darren Fielke described the eleven painstaking ground searches in inhospitable territory, which have so far turned up no useful clues – although some “anomalies” in aerial images may prompt yet another search.
Officials are hoping the state government reward of up to one million dollars for anyone with information leading to a conviction or a body will help move the investigation forwards.
Gus, described as both shy and adventurous, was last seen playing outside at 5pm on Saturday 27 September. Half an hour later, when his family went to check on him, he was gone.
His disappearance sparked one of the biggest searches the state has ever undertaken, with new searches launched as new information or theories came to light.

Volunteers, police, emergency services and defence personnel, along with dogs, divers and drones, aircraft and Aboriginal trackers scoured the 60,000 hectare Oak Park Station, about 300km inland from Adelaide.
One of the biggest moments in the search came in February this year, when Sapol declared his disappearance a major crime, and said they had identified a suspect.
Fielke said at the time they had effectively ruled out Gus wandering off or being abducted, and that they were now investigating someone in his household.
The suspect was not one of his parents, Fielke said, something he emphasised on Wednesday.

Fielke said Task Force Horizon had covered more than 700 sq km and undertaken “a painstaking, methodical, forensically detailed manual search of the aerial imagery”, which “identified some anomalies”. Those anomalies will be reviewed before any decision to start a new search is made.
Premier Peter Malinauskas said there had been “no sign of Gus”, so the government was offering the $1m reward in hopes of solving the case.
Previous state governments have offered the same amount in cases of missing children, including the three Beaumont children who disappeared without a trace from an Adelaide beach in 1966.
“We put this in place because … we spare no expense. Justice needs to be done here one way or another,” Malinauskas said.
“We will not tolerate, as a state, any circumstances where children go missing and are not able to be accounted for.”
Anyone with information relating to the disappearance of Gus Lamont is urged to contact crime stoppers.
“We’re going to continue to thoroughly and meticulously investigate the disappearance of Gus until we get a resolution,” Fielke said.

articles.title: Eleven killed in mass shooting at house in South Africa
articles.summary: One of those killed is believed to be a pregnant woman, police said.

blocks.text: At least 11 people have been killed in a mass shooting in a residential building near the South African city of Durban.

Gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township late on Tuesday and opened fire on 14 people. Ten were killed at the scene and four were taken to hospital, where one later died from their injuries, police said.
Police said some of the victims were on their watch in connection with illegal activities, which they could not "divulge at the moment to protect investigations which have been launched".
While the motive of the shooting has not yet confirmed, the police said they could not rule out a "feud between rival groupings".

"Information available at this stage suggests that 13 men and one woman, who is believed to be pregnant, were reportedly having a party inside a house when three men arrived and opened fire on them," the police said in a statement. The woman is among those who died.
A local TV reporter from the eNCA channel at the scene said the gunmen had set fire to a vehicle belonging to one of the victims before fleeing, with footage showing the burnt-out car.
The police say they have launched a manhunt for the suspects.
South Africa has one of the world's highest murder rates, with police data showing a murder rate equivalent to more than 60 deaths a day.
In recent weeks, the gruesome discovery of at least nine murdered women, with some of the bodies dumped by the roadside, has heightened fears in the country.
Last year, nine people were killed in a mass shooting at a tavern in Johannesburg.
Rivalry among criminal gangs amid turf wars, drug trafficking and illegal mining is common in the country, often driving violence within communities.

In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa said organised crime was "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development", as he announced that he would be deploying the army to support the police.

articles.title: Vince Dizon testifies in Zaldy Co flood control case
articles.summary: Department of Public Works and Highways Secretary Vince Dizon has testified before the Sandiganbayan in the case of fugitive former lawmaker Zaldy Co.

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 3:00pm

Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon joins Presidential Communications Office undersecretary and Palace press officer Atty. Claire Castro in a press briefing with the Malacañang Press Corps on Sept. 1, 2025.
The Philippine STAR / Ryan Baldemor
MANILA, Philippines — Department of Public Works and Highways Secretary Vince Dizon has testified before the Sandiganbayan in the case of fugitive former lawmaker Zaldy Co.
Dizon testified before the anti-graft court’s Fifth Division on Wednesday, September 23, in the P289.5-million flood dike project in Naujan, Oriental Mindoro, where Co faces a graft charge.

In an ambush interview with reporters on Wednesday, Dizon confirmed that he verified information showing the sheet piles used in the project were only three meters long instead of the required 12 meters.

He described the construction work done by Co-owned Sunwest Corporation as substandard, noting that during his personal visit to the site, he observed areas where erosion and excavation were already occurring after just a single rainfall.
“Pagka talaga substandard 'yung pundasyon, eh talagang 'yun ang mangyayari. So para sa'kin klarong-klaro 'yung ebidensya dito sa kaso na 'to,” Dizon said.
(When the foundation is substandard, that is inevitably what will happen. So for me, the evidence in this case is crystal clear.)
Co, who is hiding in Europe, is currently facing graft and malversation charges over the Oriental Mindoro flood control project. All of his co-accused are currently detained.

The former lawmaker is also facing a plunder charge, along with former House Speaker Martin Romualdez, for allegedly “repeatedly receiving, directly or indirectly, on at least fifteen occasions, commissions, shares, percentages, kickbacks, ‘commitments’ and/or other pecuniary benefits” worth at least P7.44 billion linked to flood control projects.

articles.title: Trump administration accuses banned media outlets of 'falsehoods' ahead of court hearing
articles.summary: The US Justice Department's response to a lawsuit filed by CNN, Politico and MS NOW also cites national security.

blocks.text: The US Justice Department has filed documents that accuse three media outlets banned from the White House of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods" and reporting which "threatened national security" as it prepared to defend the move in court.
Last week, President Donald Trump barred CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news".
After their reporters had their passes confiscated and were denied access to the building, the three outlets jointly launched legal action, calling the move unconstitutional.
On Wednesday, a judge is set to decide whether to issue an order temporarily lifting the ban, pending a full hearing.
According to a court filing by the Justice Department in a District of Columbia court, the three outlets were issued with a list of "reporting incidents" by the White House ahead of the ban.

The filing cites a number of stories about construction at the White House - including about a security bunker and the building of a new ballroom, as well as a report on an internal information leak investigation.
It goes on to say that "access to the White House is a privilege, not a right".
The three media organisations have argued that the ban breaches their rights under the First Amendment, which forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press.
In a joint statement confirming legal action against the government, they said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting.
"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."
Major TV networks have withdrawn from a media-sharing arrangement of video and images of the president, known as the pool, in protest over the ban.
Shortly after, the White House launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, which operates a 24/7 feed of clips of the president.

blocks.text: Here are the biggest headlines from India on Wednesday, September 23:

September 23, 2026
El Nino-driven heat could kill thousands in India by February: report

This year's powerful El Nino phenomenon, which is driving global heat to record levels and contributing to severe droughts, wildfires and water shortages, is likely to cause 15,800 deaths in India by the end of February, according to a research report released on Wednesday.

The warning, released by the University of Chicago-based Climate Impact Lab, said as many as 451,000 more deaths between June and February of next year could be attributed to El Nino, when compared to typical heat-related deaths in a year.
El Nino is a natural climate phenomenon that occurs every two to seven years, toward the end of the year. It comes in various strengths — depending on the prevailing conditions.

El Nino patterns are considered strong if the surface temperature of the water off the west coast of South America is over 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above average. In July this year, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) was already observing temperature increases ofgreater than 3 degrees Celsius in the eastern and central Pacific.

The Climate Impact Lab report said the powerful heat this year was most dangerous in places that are already hot and relatively poor. It projected that the Global South will see more heat-related deaths.
El Nino, regional wars fuel global food crisis
What could help prevent deaths?

Heat warnings, hydration outreach, cooling centers and a plan to cope with the heat are all ways governments can help protect people, the report said, adding that they should also expand hospital capacity and chalk out anticipatory financing.

blocks.caption: New Delhi had several cooling stations across the city in the summer of 2026. However, not all cities and towns have the same resourcesImage: Manish Swarup/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Abhiyant Tiwari, a heat expert at NRDC India who was not involved in the study, said the report's projections should serve as a call to action rather than be another reason for alarm.
But while it's one thing to have well thought-out plans — as India does — implementing these plans remains a challenge, he said.
"The real measure of our preparedness is not how many heat warnings we issue, but how effectively we protect people and reduce preventable deaths," Tiwari said.
Editing:Sean Sinico

articles.title: US and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump's 'annihilation' threat
articles.summary: The talks are the first since a ceasefire collapsed in June, with the sides exchanging fire intermittently.

blocks.text: Top Iranian and US officials have held talks at the UN in New York on a day when the US leader said he could "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if the conflict went unresolved.

No breakthrough has been reported from the meeting mediated by Qatar and involving Iran's foreign minister and US President Donald Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff - the first since a June ceasefire unravelled.
Witkoff said a round of discussions had been completed "that we hope will prove constructive and promising". Iran repeated its demand for the US to end its "acts of aggression".
The US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz.
Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to pass through the strait before the war and its closure has caused wild fluctuations of prices.
It has also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads to Congressional elections in November.

In his address at the annual meeting of the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Trump began by touting his accomplishments on the economy, immigration, the border and tackling violent crime - remarks that sounded more pitched to voters the US midterms than the diplomats in the hall.

He spent much of his address justifying the war with Iran - a huge contrast with remarks earlier by UN Secretary General António Guterres, who warned global divisions were deepening and underscored the "interdependence" of the world's peoples.

The US president argued that the conflict had prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and demonstrated the value of what he described as peace through strength - ultimatums rather than deal-making or compromise.
"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?"
Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections.
The remarks were indicative of his foreign-policy strategy of coercive diplomacy - threatening overwhelming force while keeping negotiations open.
Trump later told reporters that American officials had had a "very productive" three-hour meeting with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the general assembly.
Iran state TV confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had met Witkoff.

Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, quoted by state broadcaster IRNA, later said negotiations took part through a Qatari mediator who communicated Tehran's conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts and to US "acts of aggression".

The BBC asked Witkoff how the meetings had gone as he was leaving the UN building and he responded with a thumbs up. Witkoff later confirmed on X that the talks had been held "through the mediators, who shuttled between the two sides throughout the day".
"They successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove constructive and promising," Witkoff said. "The mediators will continue their work."
Since the ceasefire collapsed, both sides have intermittently exchanged fire.
Iran has attacked vessels it says have attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz without authorisation.
The US has attacked Iranian sites in the strait - as well as Iranian tankers off the country's coast.
The US has also maintained a blockade of Iranian ports, causing a huge disruption to the Iranian economy.

In an effort to force Tehran to agree a deal to end the conflict, President Trump has also threatened sanctions against any country that continues trading with Iran. But so far, there has been no indication of a change of course in Iran, which insists the US and Israel end their war, including against the Iran-backed Shia group Hezbollah in Lebanon which Israel has been attacking.
Yemen's Houthis - also allied to Iran - have recently intesified attacks aimed at disrupting oil shipping from Saudi Arabia, promting an escalation of the conflict with the kingdom.

articles.title: Reports of violence against women in Gaza surge, UN agency finds
articles.summary: The UN Population Fund also says there has been a "severe escalation" in the number of early and forced marriages.

blocks.text: There has been a sharp rise in reports of violence against women and girls in the Gaza Strip, including early and forced marriage, according to a series of recent reports from the UN Population Fund (UNFPA).

One report, which analyses data collected by 10 organisations, says, external the protracted crisis in war-torn Gaza has "created conditions in which women and girls face escalating risks of gender-based violence".

It also warns that there has been a "severe escalation" in the number of early and forced marriage incidents in the second quarter of this year. Both are considered types of gender-based violence (GBV) by the UN.

Another report presenting testimony from 230 women in crowded displacement camps in Gaza City and Khan Younis, external makes for a grim read, describing the violence they have experienced or witnessed.
Some readers may find some of the details in this report distressing

One displaced woman in a school-turned-shelter in Gaza highlights how rape victims are often married to their rapists to avoid shame and scandal. "When rape cases are discovered in schools, you find weddings and celebrations at the school the next day," she says.

Another woman tells how last year, at the time of famine, "a man married off his 14-year-old daughter in exchange for two bags of flour so he and his [other] children could eat". Six women in different displacement camps shared stories of such exchanges - which would have been unthinkable before the conflict between Israel and Hamas began in 2023.

Although data collection to establish actual figures remains tricky, in the second quarter of this year, the UNFPA says the number of reported cases of early and forced marriage had increased by 123% on the first quarter. Early or child marriage involved girls aged 12 to 17.

"The trends are shocking," says Nestor Owomuhangi, the UNFPA representative to Palestine. He says that the extreme circumstances over the past three years - which have seen tens of thousands of people killed, mass destruction and multiple waves of displacement in Gaza - have broken down social structures, so "everything is eroded... there is no system".

While food markets have reopened, many cannot afford the goods on offer, there is still extreme poverty and hunger with reliance on charitable handouts. Nearly all the population of more than two million Gazans have been driven from their homes, leaving most living in squalid tent camps or damaged buildings. Public services have largely collapsed, and Israeli air strikes have continued despite the ceasefire.

Prior to the war, girls in Gaza outnumbered and outperformed boys at every level of education above primary school. Now, with prolonged school closures, many children have dropped out of education. For boys there is pressure to find informal work to help support their families, for girls there are heightened issues around safety.

Living among strangers, without privacy, in a socially conservative society, there are complaints of heightened sexual harassment and abuse - many families see marrying their daughters as a way to protect them and preserve modesty. The UNFPA report - based on research carried out in late 2025 and early 2026 - reveals how girls orphaned during the war are especially vulnerable.
One woman in a Gaza City camp interviewed for the report says she attended the wedding of two girls from her family, aged just 14 and 15.

"Their uncles married them off very young. Do you know why? Because their father and mother were martyred, and their uncles wanted to get rid of the responsibility and expenses," the woman said. "By God, they don't understand what marriage or life is."

The Women's Affairs Center in Gaza - a Palestinian NGO which works with the UNFPA - and other support groups have documented distressing cases of girls who have been married and suffered abuse, often becoming pregnant. They say that those in their early teens are much more likely to have miscarriages and underweight babies than adult women.

"We see adolescent pregnancies going through the roof because of child marriage," says Owomuhangi. "A child who is at an age when the body is not fully developed to sustain another body, who is hungry, in unhygienic circumstances, who doesn't know how to take care of the infant, who doesn't even know how to take care of herself, the consequences of that pregnancy are always really, really bad."

The UN and most humanitarian organisations categorise marriages of girls under 18 as early marriage. Even before the war, this was more common among Palestinians in Hamas-run Gaza than it was in the occupied West Bank, but it was declining.

The law in Gaza allows exceptions to the minimum marital age of 17 with parental consent and authorisation by a judge. Court officials can approve marriage for those as young as 14 years and seven months old, although a local Sharia expert told us that "legal safeguards" had been removed when Islamic courts - which officiate over family matters for Muslims - were closed for a large part of the war.

The BBC has been speaking to some families in which bereaved relatives were married. Zuhair, who is 25, says his uncles pushed him to marry a 16-year-old girl from his extended family after her father - her sole guardian - was killed in an Israeli air strike.
Challenged on why he agreed to go ahead with the plan, he said: "One of the reasons that led me to marry her was that there was no one to take care of her. That's the first point."

"If it were not for the war, she would still be a young girl spoiled by her father. She would be going to school," Zuhair adds. "She still has a child's mindset, not a mature mindset. She misses school, her family, friends. She even misses simply sitting at home."

A couple says they allowed their 17-year-old son to marry his 16-year-old cousin after their older son and the girl's father were killed. The teenager is now pregnant so will not return to school. "She needs to care for her child," her father-in-law says, "her education would be in vain."

Sexual violence in Gaza remains acutely under-reported in large part due to fear of stigma and retaliation. UN safety audits have shown particular risks to women and girls at night, causing them to avoid camp toilets and bathrooms.

The latest analysis report by the UNFPA-led task force stated that incidents of sexual violence, including rape and sexual assault, "have become critical in Gaza". They accounted for 2.7% of total reported incidents of GBV from April to June 2026 - up from 2.1% in the quarter before; this represented a 61% surge in absolute case numbers.

This rise is being linked to efforts to raise awareness and provide better ways to make confidential reports. Demographic data indicated that the majority of survivors were women aged 18-59, followed by adolescent girls at 8% and adult men at 5%.

Women who are widows or have husbands who are detained or missing are at increased risk of sexual abuse and exploitation. Nearly one in four households is now reportedly headed by a woman - double the proportion before the war.

"One widow was looking for a tent, and a [camp] representative told her, "I'll give you a tent, we'll put you in our camp, and you can come stay with me tonight," recalls a woman in Gaza City, interviewed for the UNFPA report.

Aid agencies argue that the dangers for women in Gaza could be greatly eased by improving humanitarian conditions. There are calls for Israel to allow higher quality shelters into the territory as well as equipment to upgrade latrines and sanitation as well as lighting. Israel restricts items it classes as having a potential dual use for military purposes.

There are ongoing efforts to improve education and healthcare and longer-term plans for campaigns to combat domestic violence and child marriage. While the course of so many lives in Gaza has already been permanently changed, women say they hope for a future in which they at least feel safer.
If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available in the UK at BBC Action Line.

articles.title: Senate court rejects Cayetano bid to block impeach threshold vote
articles.summary: Senator-judge Alan Peter Cayetano has lost his challenge to stop the body's decision on whether to lower the math needed for Sara Duterte's conviction.

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 12:50pm

The Senate, sitting as an Impeachment Court, resumes its hearing on Monday, August 3, 2026, on Article I of the case against Vice President Sara Duterte, which concerns the alleged misuse, questionable liquidation and systematic misappropriation of confidential funds.
Senate Social Media Unit / Wendell D. Alinea

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano failed Wednesday to stop the Senate impeachment court from voting on whether to revise the 16-vote threshold for convicting Vice President Sara Duterte. Senator-judges voted 13-6, with one abstention, to reject Cayetano’s challenge and allow the threshold question to proceed.
“With 13 affirmative votes, six negative votes, one abstention, the appeal is lost,” Presiding Officer Chiz Escudero said.

The vote was not yet a decision on how many votes would be required to convict Duterte. Instead, it settled Cayetano’s attempt to prevent the impeachment court from taking up the threshold question at all.
Cayetano had raised a point of order arguing that the issue should have been settled at the start of the trial because it involved the court’s jurisdiction.
He urged the impeachment court to leave the constitutional question to the Supreme Court rather than reinterpret the threshold midway through the proceedings.
Cayetano warned that changing the number of senators used as the base for computing the two-thirds requirement could produce the equivalent of a “mistrial.”
He and Sen. Pia Cayetano had also said they would not participate in a vote on the threshold itself because they believe the Supreme Court should resolve the issue.
Escudero rejected that position and allowed the impeachment court to decide whether Sen. Erwin Tulfo’s motion to reconsider the threshold should proceed.
Thirteen of the 20 senator-judges present backed Escudero’s ruling.
Threshold question still alive
Still before the impeachment court is Tulfo’s bid to exclude four senators who have been absent from the trial from the base used to calculate the two-thirds vote required for conviction.

Escudero had ruled at the opening of the trial that 16 votes were needed to convict Duterte, interpreting the Constitution’s requirement of “two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate” as referring to the chamber’s full 24-member roster.
Tulfo’s motion asks the court to reconsider that interpretation in light of senators who are not participating in the proceedings.
If the court adopts a smaller denominator, the number of votes required for conviction could also fall.
The senator-judges are now expected to vote separately on that question.

The impeachment court had set Sept. 23 for oral arguments and deliberation on the disputed threshold after hearing differing interpretations from retired Supreme Court justices invited as amici curiae, or friends of the court. — with Cristina Chi

articles.title: Marcos admin ‘seriously considering’ absolute pardon for Mary Jane Veloso
articles.summary: Rep. Albert Garcia said the Office of the President will release an announcement regarding the matter in the following days.

blocks.text: September 23, 2026 | 12:44pm
Filipina inmate on Indonesia death row, Mary Jane Veloso (C) reacts as she arrives at the Soekarno-Hatta International Airport in Tangerang on Dec. 17, 2024, for her repatriation to Philippines.
AFP / Juni Kriswanto

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the President is "seriously considering" granting an absolute pardon on humanitarian grounds to former domestic worker and trafficking victim Mary Jane Veloso, according to a member of the House of Representatives.

House Committee on Appropriations Senior Vice Chair Albert Garcia (Bataan 2nd District) made the announcement during the deliberations on the proposed 2027 budget of the Office of the President on Wednesday, September 23.
It came after Rep. Sarah Elago (Gabriela Women’s Party) inquired about the administration’s efforts on Veloso’s release.

“The Office of the President is seriously considering granting an absolute pardon to May Jane Veloso on humanitarian grounds in support of the government’s commitment to protecting Filipino migrant workers,” Garcia said.
When asked when a decision could be expected, Garcia said the Office of the President will release an announcement regarding the matter in the following days.
Before answering Elago’s inquiry, Executive Secretary Ralph Recto was seen approaching Garcia at the podium.
Veloso’s family continues to call for executive clemency as she remains detained at the Correctional Institution for Women in Mandaluyong following her repatriation from Indonesia in December 2024.
She was convicted of drug trafficking and sentenced to death by firing squad in Indonesia in 2010 after authorities found 2.6 kilograms of heroin in her suitcase.
A last-minute reprieve was granted after the Philippine government informed Indonesian authorities about her recruiters’ surrender.
According to Elago, Veloso’s case was recognized as a human trafficking and forced drug mule exploitation case.

articles.title: Leonen to serve as acting chief justice after Gesmundo's retirement
articles.summary: Supreme Court Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen will serve as acting chief justice, while the post is vacant after the expected retirement of Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo.

Photo shows Supreme Court Associate Justice Marvic Leonen.
sc.judiciary.gov.ph

MANILA, Philippines — Supreme Court Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen will serve as acting chief justice, while the post is vacant after the expected retirement of Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo.

In a message to reporters on Tuesday, September 22, Supreme Court Spokesperson Camille, citing Section 12 of the Judiciary Act of 1948, said that “the duties and powers of the Chief Justice shall be exercised by the most senior Associate Justice until a new Chief Justice is appointed and qualified.”

“This is pursuant to Section 12 of Republic Act No. 296, or the Judiciary Act of 1948, which provides that when the position of Chief Justice is vacant, the duties and powers of the Chief Justice shall be exercised by the most senior Associate Justice until a new Chief Justice is appointed and qualified,” Ting said.
Gesmundo is expected to reach mandatory retirement on November 6. His retirement will give President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. his first opportunity to appoint a chief justice.
After his retirement, Marcos should appoint a new chief justice within 90 days from the list of nominees prepared by the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC).
The JBC has invited five senior Supreme Court associate justices, including Leonen, to apply for chief justice ahead of Gesmundo’s retirement.

articles.title: A lot has happened since the B.C. snap election was called. Here's a quick rundown
articles.summary: Cariboo-Chilcotin MLA Lorne Doerkson has become the interim leader of the Conservative Party, and MLAs who quit en masse during Kerry-Lynne Findlay's tenure are rejoining. Meanwhile, some MLAs have…

image.caption: B.C. NDP Leader David Eby is seen outside Government House in Victoria with his wife Dr. Cailey Lynch, after calling the snap election. (Mike McArthur/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New

Cariboo-Chilcotin MLA Lorne Doerkson has become the interim leader of the Conservative Party, and MLAs who quit en masse during Kerry-Lynne Findlay's tenure are rejoining. Meanwhile, some MLAs have announced they won't be seeking re-election next month.
New leaders, election dropouts, and mayors sounding off on back-to-back elections
Eby calls snap B.C. election citing 'existential' Trump threat

On Tuesday, B.C. NDP Leader David Eby put an end to weeks of speculation by calling an early election in B.C., meaning voters will head to the polls to choose their next provincial government on October 24.
Eby said the election, two years ahead of schedule, was required to meet the "existential moment" created by the Canada-U.S. trade conflict.
"We have big decisions to make as a province. And British Columbians, you deserve a say in the direction that we choose," he said in a news conference Tuesday.
But some see it as political opportunism, given the recent turmoil within the B.C. Conservatives.

B.C. Conservative interim leader Lorne Doerkson has characterised it as a "cheap, opportunistic political move," while Greens Leader Emily Lowan called it an unnecessary decision that would bring "yet more instability."
There has been a lot of political movement since the election was called.
Here's a quick rundown to help you make sense of where things are at.
B.C. Conservatives get new interim leader
Before Tuesday, Cariboo-Chilcotin legislator Lorne Doerkson wasn't a well-known name, but he has been chosen by consensus as interim leader of the B.C. Conservatives.
He wasted no time introducing himself to the electorate at a news conference held shortly after the B.C. election was called, flanked by more than a dozen Conservative MLAs.
"We are unified in one simple task, and that is to change governments in this province," he said.
Former CentreBC MLAs join Conservatives
Seven MLAs who quit the Conservative Party en masse during former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay's tenure, to subsequently join the CentreBC party, have rejoined since she was ousted on Sunday.
Peter Milobar, who departed in mid-August, spent a short time as the leader of CentreBC, but on Tuesday announced he would re-enter the Conservative fold.
Elenore Sturko, who was kicked out of the Conservative caucus in September last year, has taken over from Milobar as CentreBC leader.
She told CBC's On The Coast the Conservative Party did not align with her values.
"I want to be able to represent a portion of the voting public that feels that neither the Conservatives nor the NDP represent them," she said.
MLAs who've decided not to run
So far, three former NDP cabinet ministers have confirmed they will not be seeking re-election.
Among them is Ravi Kahlon, who currently serves as health minister.
He spent nine years as an MLA with the B.C. NDP, and did not give a reason for his departure.
"After three election cycles, I believe this is the right time for the next champion of North Delta to step forward and carry this work on," he said in a statement issued at 4 p.m. PT Tuesday.
Richmond-Steveston MLA Kelly Greene has also decided not to run again.
She was first elected in 2020, and played a key role in B.C.'s wildfire response this summer as minister of emergency management.
"This decision to step down was not made lightly," she said in a post on X.

items: Meet the party leaders running in B.C.'s provincial election

blocks.text: And on Monday, Lana Popham said she wouldn't seek re-election for what would have been her sixth term.
"I am sad to leave this role, but I am not leaving public life without purpose," she said in a statement.
B.C. mayors are not happy
The provincial election will happen exactly a week after civic elections take place in 187 provincial municipalities and regional districts across B.C. on Saturday, Oct. 17.
Local leaders are not happy about the timing, and have argued that dueling campaigns will be confusing for voters and make messaging harder for candidates.
Delta Mayor George Harvie said he was not alone in feeling "pissed off" about the situation, and Vancouver Mayor Ken Sim said it showed a lack of respect for municipalities.

Malcom Brodie, who is not running for re-election after serving 25 years as mayor of Richmond, wondered whether calling a provincial election early would anger the electorate and ultimately backfire on the B.C. NDP.
"I find this to be one of the more cynical moves I've ever seen in political life," he said.
With files from CBC News
